Sports memorabilia platform MatchWornShirt has secured fresh backing from a group of active and former footballers, alongside North American sports investors.

Announced on Tuesday, the funding round is led by Gamma Waves Partners, a global sports and technology investment platform founded by former Italy defender Giorgio Chiellini, Andrea Agnelli and Rocco Benetton.

In a recent development, former Chelsea and England captain John Terry and current Tottenham Hotspur defender Tosin Adarabioyo have invested individually. Premier League brothers Jurrien Timber (Arsenal), and Quinten Timber (Crystal Palace), have also joined the round through Joyned Capital, a private investment club for professional athletes.

Outside football, the investment group includes basketball player Kevin Durant and Rich Kleiman’s 35V, along with the ownership group behind the NBA's Indiana Pacers and WNBA's Indiana Fever.

The capital injection follows a year in which MWS expanded its physical presence in North America ahead of the 2026 World Cup and agreed inaugural partnerships in the NBA, WNBA, NFL and NHL.

MWS were founded in Amsterdam in 2017 by brothers Tijmen and Bob Zonderwijk, the idea initially coming about during a search for an Ajax shirt for their father.

The company now partners with more than 450 clubs worldwide to auction authentic, game-worn items.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“I first got involved in match-worn shirts by selling them for charity, seeing the unique emotional value these items hold for fans,” Chiellini said. “Today, it is exciting to see the category evolve, as collectors increasingly recognise the significance and value of these pieces of sporting history.

It has been revealed that “MatchWornShirt is building the infrastructure to connect fans and collectors with authentic moments from sport, while helping sports organisations unlock upcoming value from their intellectual property. We are excited to support the company's next phase of growth.”.

MWS co-founder and CEO Tijmen Zonderwijk noted the incoming shareholders align with the platform’s long-term strategy.

“The scale of the names and businesses involved in this group of investors demonstrates a collective passion for what we have already built here at MWS, and for that, we're incredibly proud,” he said.

“It also represents a shared vision for the future, and we're excited to accelerate the growth of the business whilst remaining true to our values.”.

The individual size of Terry and co's investment has not been disclosed at this time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With the controversy sparked by Felix Nmecha's celebrations after his goals in Dortmund's 2-1 win over Elfersberg last weekend, the subject was always going to be top of reporters' minds when Germany coach Jürgen Klopp faced reporters ahead of Friday's match against Serbia.

Nmecha celebrated the goals by mimicking taking a crown off his head and kneeling to place it on the ground.

This was understood by many to be a nod to a Ballers in God (SIGNIFICANT) campaign called "The King's Return.".

In a recent development, BIG, a Christian group for footballers, has noted it aims to "demonstrate love and respect towards everyone," but critics claim it discriminates against the queer and transexual people. The discourse generated by the celebration did not go unnoticed by the Germany boss.

​Klopp told reporters in Belgrade on Thursday evening, that the 26-year-old Nmecha had assured him that he meant no harm by his actions.

Sources indicate that "Last weekend I ​saw Felix score two great goals and saw the celebration and then the gesture. I thought nothing of it at the time, but then it all kicked off," he said.

"As the controversy escalated, I started looking into the details of the subject and trying to form a clear picture of it.

"I confronted him with all the things you (reporters) might have confronted him with. He told me that it had nothing to do with that at all, and that he loves all people and does not discriminate against anyone.".

He then said that Nmecha had agreed not to repeat the celebration.

In Friday's match, Klopp's goal will be to keep alive Germany's chances of reaching the Nations League quarterfinals with a win over Serbia. Germany are third in Group A2 with 5 points, trailing the Netherlands and Greece, who both have 8. Serbia, who Germany beat 2-0 in Munich last month, are still without a win.

"We feel well prepared," Klopp said, adding that his team were committed to earning "a final" for the last group last group game on Monday in Berlin against the Netherlands.

Klopp also expressed his disappointment that only a few thousand Serbian children would be admitted to the stadium due to a spectator ban. Originally, the game was to be played behind closed doors after Serbia was sanctioned for racist and discriminatory behavior by its fans. However, a clause in the UEFA rules allows a selected group of guests to attend. Now children under 15 accompanied by teachers or football coaches are expected to be at the match.

According to recent reports, "We're expecting some 5,000 guests," a spokesman for the Serbian FA told the DPA news agency. The stadium's capacity is 55,000. The German FA has been allocated just 50 tickets for its fans.

Published: 07:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 14:40 EST, 20 November 2026.

In a recent development, diet Pep is losing his fizz. Enzo Maresca may look like Pep Guardiola, may have learned his craft under his Manchester City predecessor, but his quest to follow in his mentor’s footsteps has all gone a bit flat.

Seven successive Premier League wins to start his City reign, a record for a new manager in the competition, breaking one jointly-held by Guardiola, gave the impression that this might be a smooth passing of the torch after all.

Three months in, and three defeats on the spin that left them six points behind Arsenal have made it clear that something is not clicking for Maresca.

According to recent reports, is the uncertainty around the potential punishment following that guilty verdict taking its toll? Is Maresca just suffering from his usual late autumn dips? He suffered similar tricky periods around late October and early November at Leicester and his first season at Chelsea too.

Or is there something at the heart of his side, of his system, that’s finally being exposed?

Enzo Maresca's Man City have slumped to three straight Premier League defeats after a promising start to the season.

Guardiola’s City was all about control. Keep the ball, dominate the pitch, play the game at your pace, on your terms.

Maresca’s City, regardless of how well they started the season, has been about anything but. It has been about triumph amid chaos, about moments of magic more than the overarching method.

Without that control, City’s defensive complications have been laid bare. The 13 goals they have let in after 10 games is their most at this stage since 2008. They haven’t kept a clean sheet in their last eight matches in all competitions. That's a drought longer than at any point under Guardiola.

Their biggest problem over City's three successive Premier League defeats is just how susceptible they have been to counter attacks.

Only Newcastle have faced more shots this season following ‘fast breaks’ – data giants Opta's term for counter attacks – than City’s 17, and 11 of those have come in the last three games: six against Nottingham Forest, two of which led to goals, three against Brighton and another two against Aston Villa.

Maresca’s side are being more profligate in possession, too. Over the first seven games of the season, they lost the ball 120 times a game on average – one of the best figures in the division. Since then, it’s closer to 140.

City have been wasteful in possession and regularly overrun on the counter, with Elliot Anderson (centre) too often left isolated in midfield.

ANDERSON CAN'T DO IT ALL ON HIS OWN.

It has been revealed that many of these problems have their roots in Maresca's serious problems in midfield. Rodri, the best holding midfielder of his generation, was always going to be hard to replace but Maresca appears to be expecting Elliot Anderson to do it all on his own.

In a recent development, anderson is at his best when he’s free to get up and down the pitch, box to box, using his physicality not just in winning the ball back but progressing it. No midfielder played more passes into the final third last season than Anderson at Forest. At one stage of the campaign, he had played more progressive passes than any other player across Europe’s top five leagues.

And yet Maresca is forcing Anderson to play as the sitter while his golden boy Enzo Fernandez, whom he pushed City to sign in the summer for £125million, is roaming free and high up the pitch.

Maresca likes his teams to build up in a 3-1-6 shape, which sees Fernandez push up as an extra attacking midfielder, and leaves Anderson manning the fort alone.

When City lose the ball, though, it leaves them wide open.

This is the opening goal City conceded against Forest. Josko Gvardiol wants to play the ball inside but has only red shirts and empty green space ahead of him. Anderson is the only man free, but even he is too high and has a Forest player ready to cut off the pass. Eventually, Gvardiol gets robbed and Forest score.

Sources indicate that A lack of options for Josko Gvardiol (left) led to Forest's opener against City. Enzo Fernandez (circled) was caught high up the pitch, way ahead of the deeper Anderson (also circled).

Here’s another moment in the defeat by Brighton.

The Seagulls break forward on the flank and Anderson races over to close the ball down. Fernandez is, you guessed it, high up the pitch.

City have no midfield cover to stop the ball inside, Abdukodir Khusanov gets drawn in and leaves loads of space in behind for Yasin Ayari to exploit and cross to Maxim De Cuyper for a great chance.

The lack of protection offered by Anderson and especially the more advanced Fernandez was again on show against Brighton, who were able to exploit the acres of space left in midfield.

Fernandez is doing what Maresca wants, but it’s not working. Maresca needs more from him, especially when Anderson’s instincts are to press and harass and bully, which can leave gaps when he does not yet read the game as comprehensively as Rodri.

It has been revealed that anderson sits in the top five for ball recoveries among midfielders to have played 500 minutes this season. Fernandez is in the bottom five. That figure becomes even more alarming when you consider Anderson has created more chances from open play than Fernandez, too.

It has been revealed that ayyoub Bouaddi indicated at the World Cup that he had the most similar profile to Rodri. It might be time for Maresca to put some faith in him.

In a recent development, maresca has always wanted his goalkeeper to be an 11th outfielder. In his one season at Leicester, Mads Hermansen played more passes than any goalkeeper in Championship history. During his time at Chelsea, there was a shaky moment in a draw with Arsenal when loud groans greeted a misplaced pass from Robert Sanchez.

Sources indicate that ‘I am the guy who asks Robert to do that,’ remarked Maresca after that game. ‘The moment he stops doing that, he is not going to play.’.

According to recent reports, donnarumma, though, for all his (usually) excellent shot-stopping, is anything but a ball-playing goalkeeper. The ball rolled under his foot from a simple back pass against Coventry and so nearly crept over the line. He gifted France an early lead while on international duty with Italy when he passed the ball straight to Michael Olise.

Only two keepers made more errors leading to shots than Donnarumma across the course of last season, with many of those being with his feet, like when he gifted Kai Havertz an equaliser in City's victory over Arsenal in April.

Gianluigi Donnarumma has never been good with his feet - now his excellent shot-stopping has taken a dip too.

The Italian should have easily dealt with Nicolas Jackson's second goal in City's 2-1 loss at Aston Villa.

The decision to let James Trafford leave in the summer, especially with Guardiola’s impending departure and a manager like Maresca coming in, is looking ever more misguided.

According to recent reports, trafford is not immune to mistakes either, of course. He erred badly when trying to play out from the back for City against Spurs last season and made an almost identical howler for Leeds at Bournemouth in October. But he is still far more confident at playing out from the back than Donnarumma.

The double blow for Maresca is that the trade-off with Donnarumma – where he makes up for his weakness with the ball at his feet by making saves that other keepers can’t make – is no longer paying off either.

Nicolas Jackson’s shot squirmed straight through him to hand Villa victory and condemn City to their first defeat of the season.

When you are coughing up chances as frequently as City are, Maresca needs his keeper to be on top form.

Industry observers note that do you know who is keeping the ball out of his net? James Trafford. He boasts the highest save percentage of any goalkeeper in the top flight, keeping out 81 per cent of the shots on target coming his way. Donnarumma is 15th, on less than 66 per cent.

According to Opta’s expected data, Trafford has also prevented more than four goals that he should have conceded from the quality of the shots he’s faced. Again, he’s the best in the Premier League. Donnarumma is middle of the pack.

Industry observers note that ‘At the moment, I’m not thinking about the goalkeeping situation,’ said Maresca recently. Without Trafford there and just 34-year-old Geronimo Rulli as back-up, he doesn’t really have a choice but to persist with Donnarumma and hope he improves.

When the goals stop flowing for Erling Haaland, City can't mask all their other problems.

So used are we now to seeing the Norwegian on the scoresheet, having notched nine in City’s opening eight matches, that when he goes just two games without a goal it feels as if he’s on a barren spell.

The issue, though, is less down to Haaland and more that City’s build-up in recent weeks is struggling to get him into the game.

City are finding it more difficult to get Haaland on the ball. His touches per game are falling steadily but, crucially, so are the quality of the chances his team-mates are creating for him.

Haaland had more than one Opta-defined 'big chance' in five of City’s opening seven games. He’s had just one come his way in each of their three defeats.

His expected goals (xG) tally is dropping too. Across City’s winning streak, Haaland’s average xG per match was 0.81. Only once, against Liverpool, did it drop below 0.5.

Over the three defeats, it’s just 0.45 and has not once gone above 0.5.

Antoine Semenyo missing the last three games through injury has not helped, especially when teams now try to pack the middle of the pitch and force City wide.

Haaland will come good, he always does, but City need to start serving him again if Maresca wants to get through this tricky spell and stop the vultures from circling.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • I was just a year into my international career when we qualified for my first Wafcon, which was then called the African Women’s Championship (AWC) and was held in Nigeria in 2006.
  • Sources indicate that as it turned out, it would be the game that decided who finished top of the group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an extract from the former South Africa captain’s book, she details less than ideal Wafcon 2006 preparations.

I was just a year into my international career when we qualified for my first Wafcon, which was then called the African Women’s Championship (AWC) and was held in Nigeria in 2006. I was extremely excited but very nervous to participate in this tournament, more so when it was unveiled that we would be in the same group as the hosts, and would play them last in the group.

Sources indicate that as it turned out, it would be the game that decided who finished top of the group. By then we had beaten Algeria 4-0 and Equatorial Guinea 2-0 and had to travel to Delta State to take on the hosts. I’d heard that Nigeria was the toughest country to travel to and I was about to realise why. It’s become common knowledge that South Africans and Nigerians are massive rivals on the football field but also don’t really get on off it.

Sources indicate that we felt unwelcome from the moment we arrived and we were not the only team to experience this. Nigeria exploited all avenues to play mind games with their opposition and to make them lose focus on the matches.

It has been revealed that we arrived early in the morning at the Murtala Muhammed international airport in Lagos and faced our first test: how to retrieve our luggage. Only one carousel was working, which meant we had to wait a long time for our bags to arrive. We had a training session planned for later in the day and were all eager to get to the hotel, settle in and prepare for our first practice.

According to recent reports, as we stepped out the airport doors, we looked for the bus that was to take us there, but we didn’t see one anywhere. As players, we were irritable and impatient, and starting to show it. Some of us were slumped on our bags, others had taken up residence on the pavement, and we were all cranky, especially as it took over an hour before a bus arrived.

Like in Mozambique a few years before, the bus was too small. Another 21-seater and we were 27 – 20 players and seven support staff, as well as all our luggage. Luckily, most of us had experience of how to squeeze in and so we knew the drill. We also had the advantage of our bags travelling in a smaller vehicle behind the bus, so the only challenge was fitting all the bodies in.

It has been revealed that generally, we saw the lighter side of these things and laughed as some of us got comfortable on the floor and others had to make do with a teammate’s lap. But we lost our sense of humour when we realised we had no air-conditioning and the drive was going to last at least another hour. Some grumbling ensued, but we knew better than to complain at such an early stage, and it seemed that things would get better soon.

In a recent development, when we got to the hotel, the building that greeted us looked fairly new from the outside, with freshly painted walls and a manicured garden at the entrance. But when we walked through the doors, it looked as though the hotel was in the process of being renovated, and the outside was clearly the bit that had been made up first. It still looked like a decent place, so we weren’t too worried, and the smell of new paint and the sight of workers installing lights made us feel special as the first group of people staying in this hotel.

According to recent reports, all of us were looking forward to being in our rooms and the chance to shower and relax before training. It was only when I saw maintenance workers carrying still-sealed mattresses to the rooms that it occurred to me that we were being put up in a hotel that was not fully ready for guests. I was only half-right. Actually, it was not ready at all.

When we got to our rooms, they were empty: no mattresses on the beds, no lightbulbs in the lamps and, worst of all, not a drop of water in the taps. This made us all a little worried, but we were told it would be sorted out as soon as we had finished our training. We did have lunch at the hotel, although by now I was suspicious of things and particularly of the spread of fish and chicken, and then left for training. At least that went smoothly, and we expected to get back to suitable accommodation. No such luck.

We returned to beds being made but still had no lights or running water. After a training session in extremely warm conditions, we were all dripping with sweat from head to toe and we had to make another plan. A few of our players spotted a river just outside the hotel and mentioned they were going to go there to rinse themselves off. I thought they were joking.

In a recent development, when I looked again, the players had stripped down to their tights and sports bras, wrapped themselves in their pristine white hotel towels with their toiletries in hand and were heading out the door. If I wanted to be clean, I realised, I had to join them. My hesitation was twofold: I had never washed in a river before and wasn’t sure whether it was hygienic, but I was also still quite young and didn’t want to expose my body in public. I had to get over my qualms quite quickly. Fortunately, we didn’t have to wash in the river again. No one knows how, but when we opened the taps the following day, the water gushed out.

With that kind of preparation, and Nigeria being as strong a team as they were, it was hardly a surprise that we lost 2-0. We experienced Nigeria’s off the field tactics first-hand. I did have one happy memory from the match, though. The Nigerian centre-back, Onome Ebi, who would go on to become the first African to play in six World Cups between 2003 and 2023, gave me her jersey. We both wore No 5 and she was the first international to give me her shirt. Given how much my Banyana Banyana jersey meant to me, I understood how special and symbolic this moment was, and I have stored it in my memory to this day.

Trinity Rodman's non-negotiable for Washington Spirit: 'I wouldn't be playing soccer if it wasn't fun'

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • – For 90 minutes, dedication to an organized plan is the default state for soccer players, but a postmatch celebration always has a randomness to it.
  • Rodman jumped on Kang from behind, and the owner delighted in the surprise.
  • LITERAL GOALS.Michele Kang and Trinity Rodman celebrating the Spirit way 💃 pic.twitter.com/RpTMKhTeLd.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

WASHINGTON, D.C. – For 90 minutes, dedication to an organized plan is the default state for soccer players, but a postmatch celebration always has a randomness to it. Players and team staff scatter around a field and seem to bump into each other by coincidence, a sense of enthusiastic spontaneity coming over a wide variety of people. There was no actual shock in the fact that Trinity Rodman ran into Washington Spirit owner Michele Kang after their win over the Utah Royals in the NWSL semifinals last week. The sheer joy of reaching a third straight NWSL Championship, though, took over.

Rodman jumped on Kang from behind, and the owner delighted in the surprise. The multimillionaire, clad in a chic gray cape that embodies a dignified but serious demeanor, then wasted no time clasping her hands with Rodman's and bouncing up and down. Sports team owners are hardly ever caught so candidly; no matter how much attention they do or do not attract, they are the resident corporate types, the odd ones out next to a bunch of athletes by design. For a moment on Saturday, though, Kang and Rodman were one and the same.

LITERAL GOALS.Michele Kang and Trinity Rodman celebrating the Spirit way 💃 pic.twitter.com/RpTMKhTeLd.

It was a perfect peek inside Rodman's orbit.

Rodman does not lack the seriousness that Kang exudes, her commitment to her craft just as evident as her skill. She is open to any and all questions about her job, whether they are very literally about soccer or about the nature of being the NWSL's brightest star, but not ones about aliens, which she made very clear in an interaction with a content creator on Thursday. There is a non-negotiable that's just as essential to Rodman's game as her clinical instincts in front of goal, one that is crucial to her appeal -- having fun.

Industry observers note that "I just think you shouldn't be doing anything if you're not having fun," she said Thursday, two days before playing in her fourth NWSL Championship with the Spirit. "I think I wouldn't be playing soccer if it wasn't fun for me, so sometimes it is hard to show it and to experience it because you are so focused and there is a lot of pressure, but I'm hoping to always be that person that allows us to let loose.".

According to recent reports, five years after winning the NWSL Championship at the end of a Rookie of the Year campaign, Rodman is no stranger to the league's showpiece match. The Spirit are now the finalists for a third season in a row and are still in the midst of chasing their first title since 2021, but even amid the familiarity, this year is notably different from the last. This time last year, the Spirit's headliner was battling an injury in the run-up to the final and was in the middle of negotiating what would later become a historic contract in women's soccer. She carries none of that baggage this time around.

"I'm so excited," she said. "I think going into a championship is obviously always a blessing, but going into it not 100% isn't the greatest feeling because you know that you're still going to play, but you don't know if it's going to be a great performance, so I think to be healthy and to be able to give everything that I have is really exciting for me as an individual, but also to be able to contribute to the team and get these minutes in for the last hurrah.".

Rodman has played 32 times this season and averaged 86.6 minutes per game along the way, an upgrade from 2025's tally of 17 matches and an average of 56.8 minutes per game during an injury-riddled campaign. It has allowed the 24-year-old to set the tone on the pitch, as well as off it.

"She's bubbly and brings energy to the changing room," defender Esme Morgan remarked, speaking in the build-up to the game. "She always comes in on game day and kind of screams as she enters the changing room so you're like, 'Oh, Trin's arrived.'".

There's a playfulness to Rodman that is matched by the team as a whole, so much so that, on the drive to the team's training facility in Leesburg, Va., Morgan contemplates a list of questions that feels unique to the Spirit.

"I am excited to go in every day," Morgan said. "I drive into training, and I'm looking forward to seeing the girls, and I'm thinking, 'What stupid conversation are we going to have today? What are we going to laugh about today? What silly thing are we going to do?'".

The list of silly things is endless.

"We have these significant red gym balls in the gym, like exercise balls, and we enjoy kind of throwing them at each other, whacking them off each other so it can get very silly," Morgan remarked. "I did accidentally knock [Gabrielle] Carle off one. She was bouncing on the gym ball, and I smashed one. I was aiming for a member of staff, actually. I kicked it and then missed him slightly, bounced off the wall, hit Gabby Carle, and she fell off her exercise balls, so it was funny. She was completely fine. No Gabby Carles were harmed, but that was funny, so yeah, we've been kind of going crazy with the exercise balls.".

Then there's Jose the Coyote, a plastic good-luck charm that is emblematic of Rodman's non-negotiable.

In a recent development, "I think just finding little things to get excited about, if it's as simple as Jose the Coyote," Rodman said. "Just latching onto little things that we can joke around about or have fun with, but honestly, we've been having a great time. We've been growing closer, and I think even just how many new players we've had join the roster, I think, has almost brought us closer because we do need to have more unity and language barrier and everything forces us to be closer, so I think the close-knit group allows us to have a lot more fun because we're comfortable.".

The joy is naturally rooted in something much deeper, if equally simple, after injuries have restricted her ability to focus on the task at hand.

"I think I'm just having fun in general," she noted, "because I'm playing so that's fun for me.".

Kang's interaction with Rodman at Audi Field last weekend is the type of thing that comes up in conversation unprompted, in large part because it is a snapshot of the Spirit as a club.

"Here are arguably the two people who have built us into this incredible organization with massive success," Spirit CEO Kim Stone mentioned. "It's because of the two of them. Trinity invests on the pitch. Michele invests in everything else ... [Rodman is] the only person who can jump up on Michele Kang and get her to dance and not get a different reaction from Michele.".

According to recent reports, before Rodman officially signed a deal in January worth $2 million annually, there was no question that she was worth every penny. The player is "baked into" every layer of the club's business, per Stone -- season tickets, single-game tickets, jersey sales, viewership, you name it. She is the type of player the NWSL, with much hand-wringing and a newly introduced construct following a back-and-forth with the Players Association, built a whole new rule around. It is formally called the High Impact Player rule; in conversation, in headlines and on Wikipedia, it is known as the Rodman rule. A year ago, NWSL commissioner Jessica Berman used her state of the league address to say the league would "fight" to keep Rodman around as part of a larger effort to sign and retain stars. Berman took her victory lap on Thursday ahead of another glittery NWSL Championship.

It has been revealed that "Obviously, it was incredibly notable for us to keep Trinity in this league," she said. "The fact that she's competing in the championship again is poetic, given how far we've come and all the progress we've made. It's no secret that the next generation of fans appreciates and enjoys stars and Trinity's done an incredible job of building her celebrity off the field and we are excited that she brings that to our game. It makes people want to watch. It makes people want to follow her and her story and candidly, it's our job to continue to create more of those stories so that other people are just as excited about all of the stars that do play in the NWSL.".

Rodman, though, is singular in her value to the NWSL.

In a recent development, "She's baked into the fact that we get asked to play Denver [Summit] in front of 60,000 people, to play Bay FC at Oracle Park, to play [in] Fresh York for the Queens Classic," Stone noted. "If you look at all the milestone attendance, look who the opponent is. It's every time and so she's baked into all of that. I can't quantify that off the top of my head but what I can tell you is, when I worked with Miami Heat, we had LeBron James and then when I was at Golden State [Warriors], we had Steph Curry and those generational talents, what they do for your entire organization, especially when you have a good attitude and personality like Trinity, like Steph Curry, they transform your org.

It all comes down to Rodman's non-negotiable, something that will soon become a trademark as much as the goal contributions if it is not already.

"She's fun, she's engaging," Stone said. "She's what people want to be around and they're drawn to and then she's phenomenal with fans ... If you have a personality, then we can help amplify what you're trying to do. If you are vanilla ice cream, I'm going to struggle to get a lot of people interested. If you're rocky road fudge sundae with caramel pecans on top, I got something to work with. I got some unique things. I got some fun stuff to do because what people want is just the authenticity.".

Rodman has earned the right to be the NWSL's transformational, singular talent, successfully receiving a torch that was left behind a few years ago by members of the 2019 Women's World Cup-winning U.S. team that captivated a nation.

In a recent development, "Trin is a generational talent," Stone noted. "She transcends soccer. She is arguably the face of soccer in America, men's or women's, hard stop ... What you end up with is the most popular player in our league, the most sold jerseys in our league. The people used to shout for Alex Morgan. Now they're all shouting for Trinity.".

That's according to one report, which says that the Croatian defender's departure may have begun as early as the summer, with the future of the Citizens uncertain and a potential points deduction coming after an independent commission found the club guilty of over a hundred charges of financial rule-breaking.

Manchester City have introduced an appeal – but an exodus could well be on the way, with Gvardiol the first domino.

January isn't the optimal time for transfer business, but Barcelona have interest in Gvardiol, as per AS via Sport Witness, with Hansi Flick wanting to improve his defence if he's to land a sixth Champions League title in Catalonia this season.

The report states that the Blaugrana asked about taking the 24-year-old along with Rodri while negotiating a move for the 2024 Ballon d'Or winner – but that the deal is “almost impossible” this winter due to the La Liga champions needing to raise funds to secure a major new signing.

That's where Manchester United come into play, with the Red Devils languishing in the relegation zone and having just hired Mauricio Pochettino to turn fortunes around.

United have an interest in Alejandro Balde, with the La Masia graduate failing to get the requisite playing time under Flick, and should Pochettino request a fresh full-back, the signing could well bolster the coffers for Barça to pursue Gvardiol.

Gvardiol is mentioned to be wanted by Flick for his athleticism and his ability to play both centrally and at left-back, but having signed a newly introduced deal at the Etihad Stadium over the summer, he may be completely unattainable now.

City maintain their innocence over the 115 charges, but should the club face a serious penalty, Gvardiol would surely reconsider his future, despite his recent contract extension.

The Athletic have noted that RB Leipzig’s Castello Lukeba is an option for Barcelona – as is United's own Lisandro Martinez, who fell out with club hierarchy recently over comments aimed at his team's recruitment over the summer.

The same report also mentions that United made a “deadline day check” on Balde but decided not to go any further with the deal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leeds United defender Tarik Muharemovic has emerged as one of the Premier League’s most complete centre-backs this season, ranking alongside Arsenal’s Gabriel and Ezri Konsa, and Liverpool’s Virgil van Dijk.

Data published by football analytics platform Ballity Insight Lab evaluated 54 qualifying Premier League centre-backs across the opening 10 league games of 2026/27, plotting each player’s percentile rank across two criteria: front-foot 'stopper' centre-backs and the more disciplined 'covering' centre-backs.

In the model, a stopper is measured by their ability to step out of the defensive line and win the ball, encompassing tackles, aerial duels, clearances and interceptions. Conversely, a covering centre-back is judged on positional security and composure, factoring in ball retention, recoveries and an avoidance of errors.

In a recent development, out of the 54 central defenders assessed, only four sit inside the top-right quadrant reserved for players who excel at both covering and stopping. Alongside established title contenders Van Dijk and Gabriel, as well as England international Konsa, sits Elland Road favourite Muharemovic.

According to recent reports, the numbers underline just how consistently the Bosnia-Herzegovina international has performed at the heart of Leeds’ backline. Muharemovic sits comfortably around the 77th percentile in both the stopper and cover pools, demonstrating an ability to step aggressively into challenges while also sweeping up danger in transition.

According to recent reports, stopper or Cover? Premier League centre-backs 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 🛑 Stopper CB: steps out and wins the ball. Tackles, aerials, clearances, interceptions and duels. 🧠 Cover CB: rarely beaten and keeps the ball. Dribble avoidance, ball retention, recoveries and few errors. Formula in the comments 👇 🇳🇱 Van Dijk, 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Konsa, 🇧🇷 Gabriel and 🇧🇦 Muharemović do both to some degree. 🇸🇪 Lindelöf, 🇵🇹 Dias, 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Guéhi and 🇳🇱 Van de Ven cover, but don’t stop. Needs a stopper as a partner 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Hill, 🇳🇱 Botman and 🇧🇷 Murillo stop, but don’t cover. Needs a cover as a partner.November 16, 2026.

He keeps elite firm at the top end of the chart with Liverpool skipper Van Dijk still leading the cover metric near the 98th percentile while posting around an 80th-percentile stopper score.

Konsa hovers near the 92nd percentile for covering and 88th for stopping, and Arsenal’s Gabriel posts roughly 83rd-percentile marks across both categories.

In a recent development, just as striking is the calibre of Premier League defenders who fall outside that dual-threat bracket. Several household names are classified as being better covering central defenders than stoppers, meaning they thrive at reading the game and keeping possession, but rely on a more aggressive partner to engage attackers directly.

Manchester City’s Ruben Dias and Marc Guehi, as well as Tottenham Hotspur’s Micky van de Ven all fall into that zone.

Muharemovic’s capacity to bridge both roles has proven invaluable for Leeds so far this season, and the Whites have established themselves as a tricky team to beat.

Whether it be winning first contacts against physical Premier League strikers or dropping off to snuff out balls over the top, the Bosnian's balanced skillset allows Leeds to pair him flexibly across their central defensive trio.

In a division where most central defenders lean heavily toward one side of the game, rubbing shoulders with Van Dijk and Gabriel is a ringing endorsement of Muharemovic’s rapid acclimatisation at Elland Road.

Muharemovic is valued at £33.3 million by Transfermarkt.

Sources indicate that the international break is over, and it's now time to get back to the usual business with European soccer resuming alongside the MLS playoffs in the United States. It was supposed to be a quiet break, but that wasn't the case at all, since Manchester United decided to part ways with Michael Carrick and appointed Mauricio Pochettino, who had recently signed a newly introduced deal with the United States men's national team but decided to leave after the break. Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid will battle with Barcelona for the LaLiga title, while Como are still one of the most interesting sides to watch in the near future. Let's now take a look at the five teams to watch after the break, starting with the Red Devils.

According to recent reports, the biggest change of the break: Manchester United sacked coach and club legend Michael Carrick and replaced him with Pochettino, who makes his Premier League comeback after coaching Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea. As the English giants are presently sitting 18th in the standings, this is a major task for the now-former USMNT head coach, who will make his return at Anfield against Liverpool in his opening game at United. It's a daunting start in one of the most hostile atmospheres in the country. For Pochettino, the challenge will be to strike the right balance between delivering short-term results and laying the foundations for a new chapter at the club. His ambition will be to usher in a fresh cycle at an institution that has endured one crisis after another since Sir Alex Ferguson stepped down more than a decade ago.

In a recent development, speaking of a former Manchester United head coach, Jose Mourinho has had some ups and downs early in his first season back at Real Madrid. After winning an exciting away El Clasico match against Barcelona, Mourinho's team is only three points behind Hansi Flick's side right now and is eyeing the possibility of challenging them for the LaLiga title this season. They certainly have all the ingredients to make it happen, particularly following some remarkable additions to the squad in the summer of 2026. Kylian Mbappe and Jude Bellingham are arguably entering their prime and appear ready to take the team to the next level, supported by a number of exciting young prospects who could play a key role in shaping the club's future. Will Mourinho be able to win a trophy in his first season back at the club? That would be a story.

It has been revealed that if there is one team to watch in Serie A, it's Como. The side led by Cesc Fabregas is impressing both domestically and in Europe, as it is currently fourth in the league-phase standings of the UEFA Champions League. Fabregas can count on some of the best players in the league, such as Nico Paz, the Argentine talent who is now also expected to lead the national team after Lionel Messi's retirement. The question is how far Como can go this season, given that playing every three days can be a big challenge for players who have never experienced it. They may still have to pay the price in the league, but qualifying for at least the playoffs of Europe's elite competition would remain a realistic target and, given the circumstances, a remarkable achievement in itself.

It has been revealed that it's always about Manchester City: the Citizens are still waiting to learn what sanctions they will face after an independent commission found them guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules. They are facing a challenging season that might have an impact on the years ahead. It's not clear what the sanctions will be, but we will likely know more before the end of the current season. On the pitch, they are also facing a season of changes as longtime coach Pep Guardiola left the club in the summer and was replaced by Enzo Maresca, who is now overseeing that transition.

Spanish soccer is not just about Real Madrid and Barcelona: Atletico Madrid are once again near the top of the standings, five points behind the Blaugrana. Diego Simeone, who has coached the club since 2011, is an Atletico Madrid legend who has faced so many changes over the years but has always been able to recreate the right atmosphere and environment to succeed. Atletico have changed their tactical approach and playing style many times, but they are still near the top, and that is what makes Simeone special.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Although the millions of gamers who are pulling sickies would beg to differ, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI wasn’t the most exciting midnight launch involving a sprawling enterprise full of shady characters. Over in Zurich, the clock also struck 12 on the candidate deadline for next year’s Fifa presidential election, leaving those of us who have no interest in video games with our own chaotic, multi-billion-dollar sandbox where untouchable bosses bend the rules to suit themselves. While online carjackers are busy exploring a “most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world”, football’s real-life power brokers are gearing up for a March showdown in the actual city of Rabat.

Sources indicate that for years, Gianni Infantino has looked nailed-on to glide into a fourth term of office completely unopposed, but following his disastrous Fifa Forward Enterprise wheeze to flog stakes in the World Cup to his American pals on the cheap, many of the emperor’s former allies have finally turned against him. In the wake of the revolt, European national associations withdrew their backing for Infantino and, on Thursday morning, Fifa confirmed the 56-year-old will face his first contested election since parking his backside on the throne a decade ago. Sadly for all those who would like nothing more than to see him deposed, Infantino remains the red-hot favourite in what will be a three-horse race.

In a recent development, leading the charge for the mutineers is Philippe Diallo, the 63-year-old French Football Federation president who was unanimously anointed as Europe’s preferred candidate after their actual preferred candidate, Arsène Wenger, decided not to throw his chapeau in the ring. His billing by Uefa’s vice-president, Laura McAllister, as a man “who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform” at Fifa conveniently overlooks the fact that, as recently as five months ago, Diallo’s own federation signed a letter formally endorsing Infantino again. Joining Diallo in the battle to prise Gianni’s fingers off the levers of power is Kozo Tashima, the 68-year-old honorary president of the Japan FA. He could yet stand aside to avoid a split of the vote from Fifa’s 211 members who want Infantino booted to the door marked “Do One!”. Unfortunately, Ramon Vega, the former Switzerland and Tottenham defender, won’t be on the ballot. He had again announced his candidacy but proved unable to scare up the five member-association endorsements required.

In a recent development, between now and Fifa’s March congress, all three candidates must pass a Fifa eligibility and integrity check, a feat which shouldn’t be beyond the two pretenders, given Infantino has repeatedly come through it with flying colours while helping to overhaul the committees tasked with marking his papers along the way. Assuming he once again clears the hurdle of being vetted by his own organisation, the next four months promise a familiar blur of private jets, palm-greasing and disingenuous crawling. While a generation of gamers will spend winter pulling off virtual heists in Vice City, when it comes to bending the rules in your favour, nobody plays the game quite like the Fifa final boss.

‘He wants to change lives’: the story behind Bukayo Saka’s Sócrates award

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By supporting the non-profit BigShoe, the Arsenal forward has earned deserved plaudits for his social conscience.
  • It has been revealed that valerie Fiesser will never forget her surprise when Bukayo Saka contacted her out of the blue in 2022, asking whether he could help support a project in Nigeria.
  • Four years on from that unexpected email, Fiesser was given the secret task of reaching out for a letter for Saka to read from the podium when he was presented with the Sócrates award at last month’s Ballon d’Or ceremony in London for his humanitarian work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By supporting the non-profit BigShoe, the Arsenal forward has earned deserved plaudits for his social conscience.

It has been revealed that valerie Fiesser will never forget her surprise when Bukayo Saka contacted her out of the blue in 2022, asking whether he could help support a project in Nigeria. “I remember thinking: ‘Is this really Bukayo writing us an email?’” notes the president of BigShoe, a non-profit organisation based in Frankfurt that has helped more than 10,000 children worldwide. “But that’s how he is. He’s always asking what more we can do.”.

Four years on from that unexpected email, Fiesser was given the secret task of reaching out for a letter for Saka to read from the podium when he was presented with the Sócrates award at last month’s Ballon d’Or ceremony in London for his humanitarian work. She got the words from Byiringiro, a 14-year-old from Rwanda who had his eyesight restored after having surgery thanks to a BigShoe initiative.

Industry observers note that “They told me he was going to receive the award, but he didn’t know, so they asked whether I could get a letter from one of the children we had helped,” Fiesser states. “I was really proud of Bukayo, I think the way he did it was really special. He stood there so strongly for all these children around the world that nobody sees and nobody hears. He gave them a voice. He took the attention away from himself and put it into action. That’s how I know Bukayo. It’s never about him, it’s always about the people we help. He’s incredible.”.

Saka, who donated more than 1,000 school uniforms to children in his home borough of Ealing in west London last year to help with the cost of living crisis, is understood to have heard about BigShoe from Antonio Rüdiger after the Real Madrid and Germany defender told him about some of the work he had done with the organisation, including in Sierra Leone.

Industry observers note that bigShoe has also worked with Philipp Lahm and Mesut Özil. Fiesser says Saka and his family have taken a particularly close interest in projects he supports.

It has been revealed that “When we had 150 life-changing surgeries taking place in Nigeria, he would message me asking to see pictures,” she says. “He wanted to know what was happening and whether everybody was safe. He always asks whether the team has returned safely. I don’t know how he manages to find the time, but he does.

It has been revealed that “His family are very similar. They genuinely want to make a massive impact and provide meaningful help. I wouldn’t describe Bukayo as simply a donor to BigShoe. He’s more like a member of the BigShoe team. I know that he stands behind us.”.

BigShoe was established by four friends in Germany after the 2006 World Cup. As part of its latest projects in Rwanda and Nigeria, about 3,000 people had eye examinations and were given glasses if required. “Giving a child a pair of glasses can change their life,” Fiesser states. “We also help entire families. If a father can’t see properly, he might not be able to work or read. That affects the whole family.”.

BigShoe recently renovated a school in Rwanda and provided clean drinking water through a filtration system. It has also built a library and provided private changing facilities for girls. “Once a month, some girls miss school because they don’t have suitable facilities or somewhere private to change,” states Fiesser. “We built facilities so they can continue attending school and have a quiet, private area.”.

Industry observers note that saka’s hectic playing schedule means he has yet to make a visit, but his family have been on the ground in Rwanda and he was heavily involved in funding earthquake relief projects in Morocco and Turkey. “We provided container homes for people affected by the earthquakes,” says Fiesser. “I knew I could count on him. It’s always important to Bukayo that we make a big impact. He doesn’t want money to be wasted. When I present a project to him, he wants to understand it properly. He needs to know exactly what we’re doing before he makes a decision. He’s a 100% person. Whatever he does, he gives it everything.”.

Saka’s mother, Adenike, is believed to be a driving force behind her son’s charitable work. Fiesser describes her as “one of the most amazing women I’ve met”. Plans are being made for the next projects, which include providing health insurance to families in Nigeria and food packages for children in Rwanda over Christmas, even if Saka has typically been pushing for something more long-term.

Sources indicate that “He doesn’t just want to give someone food,” Fiesser states. “Of course, food is important, and we’re providing that too, but he wants to change lives. You can help someone, but if the help doesn’t last, then it hasn’t achieved what you really wanted. If we all work together, it doesn’t matter which team we’re supporting or which country we’re helping. We’re all part of one world.”.

How Louisville City plans to tackle rare morning kickoff vs. Sacramento Republic in Saturday's USL final

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In recent years, Louisville City FC have been one of the most successful regular-season teams in United Soccer League history, but it hasn't translated to winning the substantial game.
  • Industry observers note that it's a challenge that comes with the desire to reach as many fans as possible with a final of this magnitude.
  • It has been revealed that "No, we're trying to stay on Eastern Time, so for us, it's training time," defender Kyle Adams said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In recent years, Louisville City FC have been one of the most successful regular-season teams in United Soccer League history, but it hasn't translated to winning the substantial game. They haven't won the USL Championship since 2018, and while this season has been a trying time dealing with injuries and a new coach taking over, they're playing their best soccer when it matters to set up a strange clash with Sacramento Republic at noon Eastern on Saturday. What's strange isn't that it's Louisville and Sacramento meeting, but that the match kicks off at 9 a.m. local time, a time Louisville forward Ray Serrano claims he hasn't played soccer at since he was 15. While it's a regular training time for Louisville and they'll try to keep things on an East Coast timeline, it's hard not to take the shift into account when planning for a final.

Industry observers note that it's a challenge that comes with the desire to reach as many fans as possible with a final of this magnitude. Leagues have to work with broadcast networks to ensure that the slots work, and for the USL, having the game on CBS is worth the risk of a 9 a.m. local start with a West Coast team hosting. It's nothing Louisville won't be prepared for, as they look to keep their internal clocks on Eastern Standard Time.

It has been revealed that "No, we're trying to stay on Eastern Time, so for us, it's training time," defender Kyle Adams said. "Wake up at 8:00 a.m., but really it's 5:00 a.m. Go to sleep a little bit earlier. Try to do everything really just to stay on Eastern Time, eat a little bit earlier on the night before, and just treat it as going into training, and then get after them.".

Other teams have dealt with similar issues, like the Los Angeles Rams when playing an NFL game in Australia, but it's still a struggle to deal with en route to a cup final as Louisville look to reach the pinnacle of the sport for the first time since 2018. Winners of the Prinx Tires USL Cup during the regular season, they do have cup experience that will prove to be fruitful in this competition, which Adams noted has been something that brings the injury-riddled squad together. "We know in the last few years we've struggled in these knockout games, but this year we've turned it on," Serrano stated. "It has been really good preparation, just the mentality of going into them, how we deal with the pressure, and we're seeing the fruits of all that now.".

It's cliche to say that because of the adversity that they've dealt with, the club is playing its best soccer when it matters, but between using four goalkeepers during the season and seeing manager Danny Cruz depart to be an assistant manager with Minnesota United, it hasn't been an easy task for interim manager Simon Bird to get this team on the right track at this critical juncture.

"Going back to the main part is the adversity that we've faced. You mentioned injuries, having to deal with that side of it, some of the various parts of the season, different things we've had to deal with from a tactical or technical standpoint, where we've lost games, and we feel that we shouldn't have lost games," Bird remarked when reflecting on the team's development under his leadership. "The most impressive thing I said to the guys today, yesterday in training, we worked on our defensive structure, but the whole training session I thought was excellent, not just the defensive side, off the ball but with the ball, and to see it all come together towards the end of the season is really rewarding. Hopefully, we can carry that on and put together a complete performance, and that's what we've had throughout the season-moments where we've let ourselves down in all these different areas, set pieces, maybe transition at other times, in front of goal. So, putting it all together for a complete performance on Saturday is the goal.".

Traveling away to a tough environment in Heart Health Park, Louisville will meet the hottest team in the league in Sacramento Republic. They've ridden a club-record 16-game unbeaten run to the final based on their defense. That has set a strong foundation to build on, and it could make the final one where the first team to score a goal wins the match. Sacramento's squad also has experience in USL Cup finals, which goes a long way when preparing for games of this stature.

"I don't think it can hurt to have that. This would be a step forward for my first final. I think experience is invaluable for players and for staff," Sacramento coach Neil Collins noted. "But then there's also the recognition that every game is different, every team is different, and every season is different. So it's just trying to get the balance right and enjoy the opportunity. You've got to have the mechanisms to control the things you can control. Obviously, the opposition team is trying to do the same, and we've got to do everything we can to be ready to take the opportunity when it comes. But the experience will definitely help us; there's plenty of that in our dressing room.".

Sources indicate that it's a final where the best that the league has to offer will be on display, and it couldn't come at a better time. The summer of soccer, with the United States hosting the World Cup alongside Mexico and Canada, has truly turned into a soccer avalanche, and this final showcases one of the top atmospheres in the league. You can't ask for much better than that, as no matter what, a drought will come to an end. Sacramento Republic haven't won the final since 2014, while Louisville haven't won since 2018, and for these clubs, it will mean a lot to get back to the top.

#48217. European football body’s strategy to go global leaves Fifa on tenterhooks

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1300 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

European football body’s strategy to go global leaves Fifa on tenterhooks

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1300 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Findings of ‘feasibility study’ into quest for world domination loom with Europe’s wealthiest certain to benefit whatever the outcome.
  • In a recent development, it will be one of the most eagerly devoured documents in football circles, assuming its contents are ever fully revealed.
  • Sources indicate that the study’s findings could, some leading figures in the sport’s governance believe, define football’s long-term future.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Findings of ‘feasibility study’ into quest for world domination loom with Europe’s wealthiest certain to benefit whatever the outcome.

In a recent development, it will be one of the most eagerly devoured documents in football circles, assuming its contents are ever fully revealed. In September, the increasingly powerful European Football Clubs body announced a “feasibility study” into how it can become established on a more global scale, morphing into an organisation that represents clubs all over the world.

Sources indicate that the study’s findings could, some leading figures in the sport’s governance believe, define football’s long-term future. It has the potential to transform a landscape destabilised by the scandals surrounding Fifa and Gianni Infantino.

Once considered a lobby group representing clubs’ interests in the face of domineering governing bodies, EFC has mushroomed into a behemoth with almost 1,000 members that has the potential to supplant those bodies.

It has been revealed that “Now is the time to create World Football Clubs,” the EFC chair, Nasser Al-Khelaïfi, told delegates at its general assembly in Copenhagen seven weeks ago. The desire to expand exists in plain sight and is perfectly natural, some with a close interest in the process point out, given players and domestic leagues already have their own global representative bodies.

However, others warn of “a takeover by stealth” and fear it is merely a fig leaf for the tightening of the top European clubs’ influence over the game’s shape.

Sources familiar with EFC’s intentions say it is examining how to enter the international football market as a competition organiser, floating the idea of organising more effective tournaments in different formats. That is the role of Fifa or continental organisations such as Uefa and Concacaf but, should leading clubs find a way to forge events of their own, they could reap financial and commercial benefits far beyond those on offer through the confederations.

According to recent reports, the prospect has some of the established powers on high alert. “You’re starting to see one of the major unspoken faultlines in football open up,” one source claims of EFC’s relationship with Uefa, which has become structurally closer in recent years, but is still conducted with an air of high mutual caution. “Friends close, enemies closer” is one characterisation of that relationship.

Industry observers note that this particularly appears the case now that, in the wreckage of Infantino’s doomed Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, all parties find themselves jostling for leverage. Beyond a dramatic increase in funding for the member associations, many senior figures in football have remarked that the biggest long-term consequence of FFE’s failure will be to increase the power of the biggest European clubs.

While the former development is already in motion, with Fifa announcing last month that it will hand over an additional $2.7bn (£2.05bn) from its reserves over the next four years, increasing their total investment to $6.35bn, the latter will not be far behind.

That is because EFC’s study is not alone in harbouring huge implications for football’s shape. As revealed in September, a joint venture between EFC and Fifa to run the commercial side of global club competitions like the Club World Cup has been in the works for some time, with the fallout from FFE emerging as the catalyst required to push it through.

Multiple sources say the joint venture, similar to the agreement under which Uefa and EFC have operated European club competitions since 2008 that was formalised last year with the creation of commercial entity UC3, is ready to proceed pending approval from Infantino.

One source with knowledge of the discussions claims Infantino had been holding up the deal until the FFE scandal broke in July, since when negotiations have accelerated. An announcement could be made at next month’s Fifa council meeting in Doha, although waiting until after March’s presidential election at the global governing body seems more likely.

The joint venture’s contents have caused particular concern within Uefa, whose hierarchy are believed to have made clear their wish that a deal between EFC and Fifa is not rushed through.

While Uefa have continued to attack Infantino forcibly and are on the verge of backing a candidate to stand against him in next year’s election, EFC has been largely silent since its chief executive, Charlie Marshall, sent an explosive letter to Fifa’s secretary general, Mattias Grafström, on 31 July.

EFC strongly condemned FFE, with the Guardian revealing the body threatened to boycott future Club World Cups (CWC) and withdraw its endorsement of the international match calendar. The sell-off strategy was formally dropped the following day.

One particularly incendiary section read: “Unless a fully operational Fifa-EFC CWC joint venture, with exclusive authority over, among other things, all commercial and operational matters, is established well ahead of the women’s 2028 Fifa CWC rights cycle, EFC will not support – and its member clubs will not participate in – any future edition, including the women’s and men’s 2028 and 2029 Fifa CWC.”.

Al-Khelaïfi, who is also the president of Paris Saint-Germain, did not directly address the matter during his speech in Copenhagen two months later and there are suggestions a mutually beneficial solution has been reached. The crisis may have landed EFC the terms they wanted.

“It’s not a matter of whether Gianni wins [the election], but what his mandate is, and who is behind it,” a senior source in European football said. “A large part of the answer is EFC. EFC is going to take over Fifa in the same way [it] took over Uefa. The big clubs have gained yet more power and control.

“EFC initially came out very hard against Gianni, but were quick to row back. They’ve been silent on the presidential election and other governance issues, as it’s clear they’ve reached an agreement with Fifa. The joint venture is the price of their silence.”.

Industry observers note that the result is likely to be an acceleration of trends already under way. The biggest European clubs look set to make even more money from latest tournaments, particularly given they are likely to increase in size and regularity, beginning with a 48-team men’s Club World Cup in 2029.

Chelsea earned $115m (£85m) from winning the inaugural expanded tournament last year, with six European clubs in the top seven of the prize money table and Brazil’s Fluminense the only non-European side to earn more than $50m. Solidarity payments are also skewed towards Europe, whose clubs will receive 50% of the $250m pot despite providing only 12 of the 32 contestants. Those defending the status quo note that Europe generates about 70% of Fifa’s revenue.

Recent findings suggest that A senior source at another confederation mentioned the inevitable result of the joint venture would be less money for the rest of the world, certainly in proportional terms. “The most significant long-term result of the Fifa crisis will be to entrench the economic might of the biggest European clubs,” they said. “That means reduced access to competitions, less revenue and broadcast rights for the rest of us.

Industry observers note that “The European clubs are well organised, economically rational and have taken advantage of the opportunity to extract something from Fifa. Gianni Infantino is in the business of writing cheques and will now be writing massive ones to clubs as well as member associations.”.

It has been revealed that these developments are, at least, easily foreseeable. It is less straightforward to analyse how football’s face will change if a putative World Football Clubs gains the power many believe lies in its sights. “Every club around the world deserves to be represented; to have a voice, and a better chance to succeed,” Al-Khelaïfi remarked in his September address. But the world’s wealthiest clubs stand poised to benefit from football’s crisis more handsomely than anyone.

The summer that changed Welsh football
