Crystal Palace's Ladd and Powell, of Bristol City, have played for their clubs since missing Wales' World Cup play-off semi-final games against the Albanians last month.

"For the play-off finals, just to have those experienced players back in the squad and on the pitch, I am very pleased," said Wales head coach Wilkinson.

"I think the blend of our young players and that experience is critical. The [young players] are almost naive, not understanding the play-off final pressure - it doesn't mean much to them. That's fantastic - that brings something to the group.

"Then we have the experienced heads who understand that the first leg is half-time, that a ranking is a ranking, that opposition hype is often merited, but equally they are just another team in our way.".

With 204 caps between them, Hayley Ladd (left) and Rhiannon Roberts (right) bring welcome experience to Wales' squad.

Winger Morgan had returned to action for West Ham after not being involved against Albania, but she is back on the sidelines after suffering a knee injury while playing for the Hammers last weekend.

Wilkinson remarked it is down to Morgan's club to reveal the extent of her injury.

"I haven't spoken directly to her, I've sent her a message," Wilkinson added.

"I think obviously when you pick up an injury and she's so proud of being Welsh and loves coming into camp... it's a double disappointment.

"But I'll speak to her later. Just give her some time.".

Like Southampton midfielder Hughes, Mia Ross â who is without a club after leaving Charlton in September - is again missing from Wilkinson's squad, while Fulham full-back Charlie Estcourt is another absentee.

There is also no place for Sunderland defender Tara Bourne, who has switched allegiance from England to Wales, but is injured.

There is a recall for once-capped teenager Gwen Zimmerman, who plays for American side Northwestern NCAA, while Newcastle youngster Casi Gregson is included again after winning her first cap against Albania.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Simone Magill's return is a significant boost for Michael McArdle's side.

Northern Ireland manager Michael McArdle has made five changes to his squad for the upcoming friendlies against Greece, with the return of experienced striker Simone Magill among the notable returnees.

Magill, who gave birth to her daughter Skye over the summer, returned to training with the Northern Ireland squad last month but did not play in either leg of the World Cup play-off defeat by Portugal.

The 32-year-old Birmingham City forward has not represented Northern Ireland since announcing her pregnancy just over a year ago and will now be hoping to add to her 95 caps and 28 international goals.

According to recent reports, glentoran midfielder Chloe McCarron returns after an injury-hit spell, while Hibernian's Joely Andrews is also back after missing the Portugal games through injury. Both featured for Northern Ireland at the Euros in 2022.

Kerry Beattie completes the trio of returnees in the 24-player squad after impressing in front of goal since joining Portsmouth from Aberdeen during the summer.

'You can be a mum and a footballer - they can co-exist'.

Family, football and Dalglish - what drives NI boss McArdle?

Industry observers note that there is also a senior recall for defender Ella Haughey. The 22-year-old West Brom player last received a call-up in 2021, when she was named among the substitutes for friendlies against England and Scotland.

Meanwhile, Kess Elmore, Jane McMaster and Lucy-Jayne Grant have retained their places after receiving their first senior call-ups last month.

Injured defender Natalie Johnson misses out, alongside Mia Moore, Naomi McLaughlin, Charlotte Havern and Leyla McFarland.

Both matches will take place at Inver Park in Larne, with the first meeting scheduled for Friday 27 November before the sides face off again on Tuesday 1 December.

Northern Ireland currently sit 52nd in the Fifa world rankings, six places above Greece.

The Birmingham City forward's return has been carefully managed through close collaboration between Northern Ireland and her club, with both parties keen to ensure she is given the time and support needed to make the transition back into competitive football.

Michael McArdle was delighted to welcome his captain back into the fold, revealing that Magill's family were also involved in the previous international camp as she began preparing for life as a mother and professional footballer.

"I'm delighted we've got our captain back," McArdle told BBC Sport NI.

"We've had on the last camp Simone, her husband Mark and Skye as well, just as a transition for us all to get ready for the future for Simone as a mother athlete now.

It has been revealed that "That's the exciting piece for her, but great to have her back in a playing capacity now. No pressure or expectation for Simone. It's part of the process collaboratively between us and Birmingham.".

Magill also had the opportunity to get back on the training pitch during the previous camp, taking another important step in her gradual return.

McArdle explained that considerable work has been taking place behind the scenes at Birmingham City, with the club's performance staff working closely alongside Northern Ireland's team to manage her progress.

"There's a lot of work going on at the club just now to support Simone's return," he mentioned.

"This opportunity to be in camp and selected again is that opportunity to take that, hopefully playing minutes as well.".

Although she has yet to make a public appearance for Birmingham this season, McArdle confirmed that Magill has continued working and gaining minutes behind closed doors.

"We've been very close with Birmingham since pre-season, so Birmingham's performance team and our performance team work together," he added.

Sources indicate that for Northern Ireland, however, her return is about more than simply adding another player to the squad. Magill's experience, leadership and influence remain hugely key.

"Her presence, obviously, is our captain and our leader within the playing group, for us as staff as well," McArdle mentioned.

With no expectations placed on her immediate playing involvement, the priority is ensuring Magill's comeback happens at the right pace, while allowing Northern Ireland to benefit from having their captain back among the group.

Published: 14:02 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 16:24 EST, 20 November 2026.

NFL icon Tom Brady has purchased a small stake in Premier League giants Chelsea, according to ESPN.

It would see the seven-time Super Bowl champion make a swift return to investment in English football after he stepped away from Championship leaders Birmingham City earlier this month.

Brady was in attendance at the MetLife Stadium in Fresh Jersey when Chelsea beat Paris Saint-Germain 3-0 in the 2025 Club World Cup final.

The New England Patriots icon, who also owns a minority stake in the NFL's Las Vegas Raiders, reportedly has a good relationship with Behdad Eghbali, who oversees the club’s Clearlake Capital ownership.

Chelsea declined to comment when approached, but sources have stood up the negotiations.

Brady, the greatest quarterback of all time, secured a minority stake in Birmingham in August 2023. That followed Tom Wagner purchasing a 45 percent stake at the club earlier that same year.

NFL icon Tom Brady has purchased a small stake in Premier League giants Chelsea.

Brady watched Chelsea beat Paris Saint-Germain 3-0 in the 2025 Club World Cup final.

At Birmingham, Brady made headlines when he questioned Wayne Rooney’s work ethic during a documentary following his time at St Andrew’s.

Rooney, who went on to be sacked after just 15 games in charge, later described those comments as ‘very unfair’.

In a recent development, when Brady exited Birmingham, the club mentioned in a statement: ‘Birmingham City Football Club expresses its sincere gratitude to Tom Brady for his involvement with and unwavering support for the club over the last three years. It was truly amazing to have someone with Tom’s experience and passion associated with the club, and the club looks forward to continuing to build on that foundation from the training ground to the Birmingham community.’.

Chelsea have invited minority shareholders with their women’s team.

NBA star Giannis Antetokounmpo previously purchased a stake in the side, partnering with Alexis Ohanian, the founder of social media platform Reddit who likewise invested in the team in 2025.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Derek McInnes joined Rangers from Hearts in the summer.
  • Manager Derek McInnes notes Rangers will only sell a player in the January transfer window if they receive an offer that "makes the club blink".
  • Players such as German striker Ryan Naderi, Mauritania winger Djeidi Gassama and Belgium midfielder Nico Raskin have been linked with moves while centre-backs Olwethu Makhanya and Emmanuel Fernandez have attracted interest after their starts to the season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Derek McInnes joined Rangers from Hearts in the summer.

Manager Derek McInnes notes Rangers will only sell a player in the January transfer window if they receive an offer that "makes the club blink".

Players such as German striker Ryan Naderi, Mauritania winger Djeidi Gassama and Belgium midfielder Nico Raskin have been linked with moves while centre-backs Olwethu Makhanya and Emmanuel Fernandez have attracted interest after their starts to the season.

However McInnes will oppose moves for players who have featured regularly in his first season in charge at Ibrox - unless a club makes a startling offer that is too good to turn down.

"If somebody comes in way over the top then you have to obviously consider these sort of things," he remarked.

Industry observers note that "But in the main, we're not looking to move players out, particularly players that have been playing regularly. We want to shut that down really early.

"We don't want agents flirting with clubs, giving them any encouragement. We know and understand that keeping that core of players and having that stability is so important for us.

According to recent reports, "We don't want January window to be excitable or dramatic. Just to come and go and hopefully we can just keep doing what we're doing.".

McInnes mentioned that Lawrence Shankland and Cammy Devlin are progressing well in their rehabilitation and that his players returned unscathed from international duty - although Kevin Kelsy was back later than expected from the Venezuela squad.

"Kevin is the only wee anomaly. We didn't get him back from Russia on Wednesday night because of a few concerns with transport, but we managed to get him back in at lunchtime on Thursday," McInnes stated.

Rangers face Motherwell in Lanarkshire on Saturday and have a solid away record - but dropped points in two away draws prior to the win at St Mirren.

McInnes is expecting a stiff test as he believes the Steelmen are beginning to perform like the side that impressed throughout last season and qualified for Europe.

According to recent reports, "I think they have got a lot of traits and similarities to the team that got a lot of success last year. I think over the last two or three games they've started to look a wee bit more like that," he added.

"They'll be a difficult opponent, but if we want to get to where we want to get to this season, we want to make sure we leave Motherwell with all three points.".

The authors retract this article, following a suggestion from the editors. Shortly after publication, a preprint (subsequently published (see ref. 1 below)) by Till Sawala identified an inconsistency in our analysis. Ice hockey impasse as Russia threatens sanctions on Canada, Germany

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (631 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Should Canada and Germany refuse to allow the Russian team to participate, we will demand compensation, enforce the postponement of the competitions, and impose sanctions on the organizers," Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak told the TASS news agency.
  • "There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed," Tretiak noted after a presidential sports council meeting in Moscow on Thursday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Should Canada and Germany refuse to allow the Russian team to participate, we will demand compensation, enforce the postponement of the competitions, and impose sanctions on the organizers," Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak told the TASS news agency.

"There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed," Tretiak noted after a presidential sports council meeting in Moscow on Thursday.

"The IIHF as a way out — either allow us to participate or, if we cannot enter Canada, move the championship, don't hold it at all, or impose sanctions on Canada.".

The threat comes after the Canadian government confirmed Wednesday that it would not allow Russian players to take part in the IIHF World Junior Championship starting on December 26 in Alberta.

"Canada's position is unequivocal: as long as Russia continues ⁠its war of aggression ​against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual," Adam van Koeverden, Canada's secretary of sport, said in a statement on Wednesday. "Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine.".

Following the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling in late October, in which it said the security concerns the IIHF cited for barring Russian teams from taking part in international tournaments was not sufficient, the world governing body pledged to work to comply with the decision.

It has been revealed that on November 8, Norway said it had been bumped from the World Juniors tournament and had been informed by the IIHF that Russia would take its place. Several other national hockey associations said they had received a revised schedule for the tournament and stated they would not play against Russia. The IIHF has not confirmed the change.

Germany has been watching developments related to the World Juniors and host nation Canada closely, as it is set to host the IIHF World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf starting on May 14.

With several nations saying they will not play Russia and major sponsors threatening to pull out, a German government spokesman described the prospect of hosting the tournament under these conditions as "effectively impossible.".

However, Germany has ruled out taking the Canadian approach.

Ronald Rauhe, Germany's minister of state for sport, mentioned Wednesday that refusing to grant visas was "not a solution for the [German] ice hockey federation [DEB], nor is it a solution for successfully hosting a world championship anywhere.".

At the same time, though, he expressed support for the DEB in its wish to host the tournament as planned.

"We believe that we should channel all our energy and efforts into helping sport — and ice hockey in particular — find a solution, which would, of course, entail excluding Russia from the World Championship.".

What makes things even more complicated for German officials are concerns that taking a hard-line on Russia could jeopardize Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

In a recent development, the thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees bidding to host an Olympic Games to follow its lead. The IOC is set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process.

It has been revealed that for now, though, the ball appears to be in the IIHF's court, after Ottawa confirmed its refusal to grant Russians visas to play in the World Juniors. How the dispute regarding that tournament gets resolved could go a long way to finding a solution for the men's tournament in Germany in May.

Timing is everything in football - and that goes for getting transfer moves right, too.

After seven years at Chelsea, Willian made the move across London to join Arsenal in 2020, which seemed like it should be a decent enough fit for all concerned.

But Willian has made no secret of the fact that he did not enjoy his time at the Emirates Stadium - and in hindsight, he believes he may simply have been the wrong player in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Sources indicate that willian told FourFourTwo: "These things happen in football. I had some personal frustrations and I couldn't perform on the pitch the way I had been performing at Chelsea.

According to recent reports, "Arsenal were also a club that was changing a lot at that time. There were a lot of people leaving and a lot of fresh people coming in.

"It was a restructuring and I got caught up in the middle of it - and it's not easy.

I left a well-established club, winning almost every year, fighting for titles every year, and I joined a club that was trying to find a way to win titles again.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"So I got caught up in that situation, and that's why things didn't work out. It wasn't easy, but I really wasn't happy.

"The contract I had was actually a very big one, but it got to the point that money wasn’t enough.

Recent findings suggest that "The most vital thing is to be happy, to play with joy. I wasn't able to do so there, so I ended up asking to leave the club, leaving that contract behind.".

After spending a year back in Brazil with Corinthians, Willian found a upcoming home at Fulham in 2022 - and he credits Marco Silva with helping him to rediscover his spark.

He remarked: "When I left Brazil, my goal was to go to England, stay there, because I love the place and my agent lives there too.

According to recent reports, "Therefore, I decided to be in London, have some meetings and see what the possibilities are. My agent noted, ‘Marco Silva wants to talk to you’. We had a meeting with him, and he invited me to join training and see how I felt.

"It wasn't a trial, it was more to see if I could readjust, especially after what had happened to me at Arsenal.

"I really liked Marco’s style. I felt celebrated, and it's not flattery, but I felt that respect, that affection from everyone. I was very happy there at Fulham.".

Tech Report: Odegaard winner spares officials from bizarre VAR row

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4045 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An ultimately routine Arsenal win but, even by the standards of VAR, an utterly bizarre refereeing controversy.
  • In a recent development, the major talking point arose with inadvertent theatre from referee Farai Hallam when Kai Havertz, who was clearly in an offside position, was equally clearly pulled down by Hull City defender Nobel Mendy inside the penalty area.
  • Sources indicate that “After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No 32 on Red No 29,” the referee declared.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An ultimately routine Arsenal win but, even by the standards of VAR, an utterly bizarre refereeing controversy. Mikel Arteta’s instant simmering fury at being denied a first-half penalty may also have turned into something rather more explosive had Martin Odegaard not later sent the champions six points clear with a ninth win in 10 Premier League games.

In a recent development, the major talking point arose with inadvertent theatre from referee Farai Hallam when Kai Havertz, who was clearly in an offside position, was equally clearly pulled down by Hull City defender Nobel Mendy inside the penalty area. Which came first? The intervention of VAR suggested the latter. But Hallam duly went to check the pitch-side monitor before then announcing the former.

Sources indicate that “After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No 32 on Red No 29,” the referee declared. Cue cheers from the home Arsenal crowd. “However…,” he went on. “Red No 29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City.”.

It has been revealed that #ARSHUL – 42' VAR recommended an on-field review for a potential penalty to Arsenal for a challenge by Mendy on Havertz - but determined that Havertz was in an offside position in the build-up. REF: "After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No.32 on Red No.29. However, Red No.29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City".

Industry observers note that it all sounded so decisive that most inside the Emirates instinctively thought the outcome reasonable. But then came a closer look at the rules. And Law 11.2 certainly did seem to support Arteta’s protestations: “In situations where a player in an offside position is moving towards the ball with the intention of playing the ball and is fouled before playing or attempting to play the ball, or challenging an opponent for the ball, the foul is penalised as it has occurred before the offside offence.”.

Sources indicate that arteta clearly saw no value after the match in aiming much criticism at Hallam following a fourth 1-0 win in 10 league games, but did still emphasise his surprise at the decision. “What do you think?” he asked one reporter. “I thought offside, but the law says that doesn’t matter,” replied the journalist. “So not offside then,” mentioned Arteta, who stressed that he needs to understand “what is overruling what in the decision-making” after a Premier League statement simply said that Havertz was deemed offside “in the build-up”.

It has been revealed that at the very best, it all leaves further confusion and again opens refereeing body Pro Ref to the charge of inconsistency. Fabian Schär, for example, was awarded a penalty for Newcastle against Bournemouth in 2024, despite being in an offside position when his shirt was grabbed by Adam Smith.

It has been revealed that conversely, Dango Ouattara had a penalty overturned for Brentford against Leeds last season after going down under pressure from Gabriel Gudmundsson before being deemed offside. The crucial point seems to be whether the player has actually challenged for the ball at the time of the infringement and, in this case, the answer was surely “no”.

Recent findings suggest that premier League title triumphs, however, are often forged on forgettable wins in frustrating circumstances and this was ultimately a classic of the genre. With Noni Madueke continuing to step up superbly in the absence of Bukayo Saka, Arsenal’s combination of attacking persistence and defensive resilience was ultimately rewarded by Odegaard’s scrappy 72nd-minute shot. For young players, it was also every bit as educational as the VAR controversy might be for emerging officials.

Madueke’s low shot forced a save by Hull goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis, but Odegaard was somehow first to the rebound, despite being the wrong side of the penalty spot and five yards behind Hull defender John Egan when the ball was struck.

“The way he scores, not the most beautiful, but the most effective,” stated Arteta, who said that his team had sometimes tried too hard for a “perfect goal” and should instead be happy with something “more pragmatic”.

According to recent reports, it was a well-judged assessment as Arsenal head into the international break with creative deficiencies, but still almost flawless in the cold hard currency of results. Three wins in three days, including at Anfield and in Prague, also underlines a certain champions mentality.

Industry observers note that “I need to praise the players,” remarked Arteta. “It’s been very very demanding; very short time to recover with all the travel. The mentality is incredible. It’s still going to be super difficult. We can improve in a number of areas.”.

In a recent development, when it was then put to him that Arsenal have been offside 35 times this season – with Havertz responsible for 15 of those – Arteta acknowledged that “timing” was one element. But, with Havertz targeted by some frustrated fans, he stressed that responsibility was always shared for those split-second moments by the passer and receiver.

He also singled out Madueke, again easily Arsenal’s most creative player, following his surprise omission from Thomas Tuchel’s England squad. “He went away, started to train, he came back and it was a different Noni,” noted Arteta, of his reaction to also being out of the Arsenal team earlier in the season. “You could sense that he meant business and he wasn’t going to accept the situation and, since then, I think he’s been incredible.”.

An improved showing by Jaissle’s Newcastle, but they will be dissapointed that they failed to see it through after Jacob Murphy scored in the 80th minute.

Recent findings suggest that arsenal far from their best, but it is another one-goal win in the Premier League. They are now six points clear at the top of the Premier League, and it is 27 points from the first 30 available.

Another save at Craven Cottage, this time from Hornicek to keep out a sweet strike from Sessegnon at the edge of the box. Moments earlier, Dedic brought down Muniz at the edge of the box.

Industry observers note that one last change by Arteta: Zubmimendi on for Guimaraes. Madueke could have made the points safe after slick interplay involving Eze and Merino around the edge of the box. Tried to be clever with the finish, the goalkeeper’s save was deflected back towards the goal and it was hacked off the line.

Leno gets down swiftly to deny Lewis Hall as Newcastle pour forward in search of the winner.

As good as Murphy’s goal was, Rodrigo Muniz’s finish with the outside of his foot may well be better. Newcastle’s lead was short-lived.

And they have immediately conceded an equaliser, Rodrigo Munoz with a smart close range finish but Newcastle were be mortified with the defending.

Not for the first time Will Osula’s weak hold up play gives the ball back to Fulham but Newcastle had plenty of men back and failed to clear.

Jacob Murphy has scored the goal that some of Newcastle’s earlier good play deserved. Cut inside on to his weaker left foot, and curled a shot beyond Leno from 20 yards.

Newcastle finally have their goal and what a strike it is from Jacob Murphy. A loose pass from Cesar Palacios in midfield gifted possession to the Newcastle winger and he ran forward, cut inside on to his left foot and curled a shot beyond the reach of Leno from 25 yards.

In a recent development, arsenal’s captain dinks over Tzolakis after Hull’s goalkeeper saved Madueke’s shot. Odeegard was on the move while the defenders were on their heels. Relief at the Emirates, this has been hard work for the champions. Can Hull muster a response?

Industry observers note that this is about as dominant as Newcastle have been in a game all season but they have not been able to find a goal from some where. They have just gone close again as Will Osula just fails to reach Amar Dedic’s cross.

Arteta has made another double sub: Hincapie and Eze replace Tzolis and Calafiori, so all change down the left flank. For Hull, Lucas Herrington has replaced the injured Semi Ajayi at the back.

Felt like the cheers for Viktor Gyokeres to replace Kai Havertz were as much a reflection on frustrations with the German as enthusiasm for the Swede. Havertz has struggled today and is far less convincing in this sort of match – when the onus is more on the Arsenal to create – than he was in scoring the winner at Anfield last Sunday.

Specific explanation for Declan Rice’s substitution is unclear – he didn’t look injured – and so perhaps just reflection of risks associated with a third 90 minutes in six days alongside an acknowledgement of quality alternatives on the bench.

Some changes at the Emirates: Cho and Lewie Coyle are replaced by Joe Gelhardt and Brooke Norton-Cuffy.

Arteta with a double sub: Gyokeres and Merino on for Havertz and Rice, which comes as something of a surprise.

Hull’s goalkeeper Tzolakis has just saved with his feet to deny Madueke. A few minutes earlier, Konsa blocked a Cho shot after a threatening Hull break. Still no opening goal.

In a recent development, it has been all Newcastle at the start of the second half and Harvey Barnes has now failed to take a hat-trick of chances. This was the best of the lot, running on to the ball, middle of the area from a perfectly weighted Yoane Wissa pass, he blasted a shot the wrong side of the post.

Sources indicate that the second halves at the Emirates and Craven Cottage have kicked off. No changes from Arsenal, Hull, Fulham or Newcastle.

While Kai Havertz was in an offside position when his shirt was pulled, he may not have been active.

The law states: “A player in an offside position is moving towards the ball with the intention of playing the ball and is fouled before playing or attempting to play the ball, or challenging an opponent for the ball, the foul is penalised as it has occurred before the offside offence.”.

However, the Premier League match centre does not see it that way.

Recent findings suggest that #ARSHUL – 42' VAR recommended an on-field review for a potential penalty to Arsenal for a challenge by Mendy on Havertz - but determined that Havertz was in an offside position in the build-up. REF: "After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No.32 on Red No.29. However, Red No.29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City".

Frustrating first half for Arsenal, but it was never going to be easy to go again in the Premier League following a Champions League away game and last Sunday’s big win against Liverpool. Hull have also played with confidence and resolve.

Hopefully there will be more action in the second 45 minutes at Craven Cottage and the Emirates.

An odd moment at the Emirates. Referee Farai Hallam was sent to monitor to look at a shirt pull on Kai Havertz in the Hull box. Through his headset, he tells the crowd that a “holding offence” has been committed – cue cheers from the Arsenal fans – before adding “however, the Arsenal player was in an offside position”. So no penalty. It would have been very soft in any case, Havertz was not close to reaching the rebound from a long shot.

Mikel Arteta predictably furious to not get a penalty, even though Havertz was clearly offside before being pulled.

According to recent reports, I’ve spotted something else since I was covering Arsenal in 2018. I was gazing up at the boards that circle the top tier where the club mark every trophy that the team has won. There was previously this big gap, of course, from 2005 until 2014 before the cabinet gradually began refilling. But someone has since had a good idea. They have added all the women’s trophies as well, transforming the tally by just the odd 17 during those tricky years of transition and billionaire rivals owners in the men’s game.

Declan Rice has also just had a shot flash wide, but still no clear chances for either team.

Dan Burn thought he had scored from close-range, but Wissa has been penalised for blocking Castagne so the goal was ruled out.

Sources indicate that #FULNEW – 33' The referee's call of no goal to Newcastle United was checked and confirmed by VAR – with it deemed that Wissa fouled Castagne in the build-up. AR2: "Defensive foul at the back post. Wissa holding at the back post". REF: "Castagne held back by Wissa. It's a deliberate foul". VAR: "He's clearly holding him - confirming the on-field decision of defensive free-kick. Wissa is clearly making an attempt to hold the Fulham defender. Clear holding offence".

Some controversy here as Newcastle appear to have had a perfectly good goal ruled out for an innocuous looking foul from Yoane Wissa on Timothy Costagne inside the box. Dan Burn was the scorer. Newcastle’s bench are furious. Most of us are just bemused.

Industry observers note that arsenal have largely been on top after Hull’s lively start but clear chances are scarce and Hull’s fans certainly sound increasingly confident. “You’re only here for the Tigers”, they say. To which a rendition of “champions” rings out. On that note, they had a replica of the Premier League trophy outside the Emirates before the match, with fans queuing up to get their photo with it.

Industry observers note that the bright start from the visitors has not been maintained and Fulham have been on top for the last few minutes. Lukasz Hornicek just made a full-stretch save to deny Oscar Bobb and there is a sense inside the stadium that the first goal is coming.

Newcastle, as we have seen all too often recently, really struggle to pass through the lines and when the ball makes it out wide it invariably seems to go backwards again.

Although Harvey Barnes has just forced a good save from Leno from a Jacob Murphy cross. It was easily Newcastle’s best move of the match as Wissa and Osula linked up for the first time through the middle.

In a recent development, david Raya to Arsenal’s rescue, plucking Stroud’s shot away from the bottom corner after a Calafiori giveaway. This has been a positive opening 20 minutes from Hull.

Arsenal with a penalty shout, turned down.

Kai Havertz was going away from goal but Nobel Medy hardly subtle with his challenge – arm and leg – on the edge of the area. It would have been what we call soft but the sort of innocuous challenge that very often results in a foul elsewhere on the pitch.

In a recent development, on a self-indulgent note, this is an all-too-rare trip to the Emirates for me. I covered Arsenal for the last decade of the Arsene Wenger era, ending in 2018 and haven’t made many visits since. A few things are already striking: so many familiar faces still among the staff at a club that has always had more of a family feel than most. Outside, and few of the gaps in the middle (or top tier) that became evident during the final Wenger years when many fans clearly lost faith in the team’s title-winning credentials. The atmosphere is a notch up too.

Sources indicate that thiaw heads wide after a well-worked short corner from Newcastle, but the flag is up for offside in any case. Lewis Hall with the cross.

Industry observers note that A decent start from Newcastle United against Fulham and you can see clearer patterns of play emerging. The fact that Fulham are constantly looking to build their attacks by playing out from the back has also helped. The home side have had a couple of scares already.

Hull gain some territory in the early exchanges, and win a corner via a long throw. From the set-piece, Egan’s set-piece hit the side-netting. A shot across Arsenal’s bows.

According to recent reports, the lack of Mohamed Beloloumi’s creative spark clearly a big blow for Hull against the best defence in the league; a defence that will be further strengthened by the imminent return of William Saliba. Mikel Arteta had decided that Saliba would be better served by playing against Aston Villa for the Under-21s at Boreham Wood tomorrow. Hull have started on the front, though, in the opening minutes.

It has been revealed that updates to follow from the Emirates and Craven Cottage. The Last Post was played and there was a minute’s silence as both grounds mark Remembrance Day.

It’s always great to be back home. It’s the last game before the international break so we know the importance of that and the challenges Hull will provide today. We’re super focused, it’s a massive game for us.

With the amount of games we’re playing, we need that freshness. The team has been performing really well, the finishers have been key again and that’s what we have today – start the game really, really strong and if we need to, have the ability to change the game.

Arsenal’s manager indicates the centre-back will play an Under-21s game tomorrow as the continues his recovery from a back injury.

Arteta indicates: “In regards to Willy as well, he needs some minutes. Obviously, the Champions League allows you to bring more players into the bench, but we believe that it’s the best thing to do: to play some minutes at the weekend with the Under-21s and then be fully fit for the international break.”.

Arsenal are playing very good football, no matter Champions League or Premier League. They are very strong, they control everything not just against us, also other better clubs. But in football, we have a chance. Obviously, they are a massive favourite, and we can start to try to create some difficulties for them.

The return of Sean Steur is a positive move from Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle but is it also a sign the German is feeling the pressure of public opinion on Tyneside?

The 18-year-old has looked the best of Newcastle’s summer signings but Newcastle are understandably trying to ease the teenager into things.

Ultimately, though, Steur is the only midfield player who can take possession of the ball under pressure and despite his tender years they have looked a better side with him in it.

There have been widespread calls for Steur to be called back into the side and Jaissle has done just that for a game he could really do with winning coming off the back of four defeats in their last five games.

Malick Thiaw also comes back into the side for Fabian Schar, with Jacob Murphy preferred to Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa starting in place of Joe Willock. I don’t think any of those dropped can have any complaints.

According to recent reports, however, the constant chopping and changing betrays the problems Jaissle is facing. Whatever team he sends out is struggling to deliver what he wants, both individually and collectively.

With the international break coming up, Newcastle need a positive result to quieten the negative noise.

Fulham XI: Leno; Castagne, Affengruber, Bassey, Robinson; Berge, Charles; Bobb, King, Iwobi; Garcia.

Subs: Lecomte, Tete, Andersen, Palacios, Muniz, Kevin, Larsson, Angel, Sessegnon.

Newcastle XI: Hornicek; Dedic, Thiaw, Burn, Hall; Steur, Gonzalez; Murphy, Wissa, Barnes; Osula.

Subs: Pope, Livramento, Botman, Schar, Toure, Elanga, Fernandez-Pardo, Willock, Miley.

Sources indicate that A significant blow for Hull to be without their most inventive and dangerous attacking player. It looks like Sergej Jakirovic has switched things up with a 5-3-2, and it will be a back five not a three for long periods.

Hull XI: Tzolakis, Coyle, Ajayi, Egan, Mendy, Stroud, Slater, Iroegbunam, Gourna, McBurnie, Cho.

Subs: Butland, Giles, Thomas, Gelhardt, Hjerto-Dahl, Norton-Cuffy, Herrington, Mouzakitis, Vaz.

In a recent development, no William Saliba in the squad despite his inclusion in the Champions League, although you are allowed more subs on the bench in that competition. Otherwise, Arsenal as expected with Arteta deciding against picking a team without Rice.

Arsenal XI: Raya; Timber, Konsa, Gabriel, Calafiori; Rice, Guimaraes, Odegaard; Madueke, Havertz, Tzolis.

Subs: Kepa, White, Mosquera, Hincapie, Lewis-Skelly, Zubimendi, Merino, Eze Gyokeres.

🔴 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 ⚪️ Let's get it, Gunners 👊 🤝 @deel.

Mikel Arteta has mentioned Arsenal are “looking after” Declan Rice more now than in any previous campaign and has rejected suggestions that the England midfielder is being overplayed.

Rice played through nerve pain in his hamstring in the second half of last season, when he made an extraordinary 69 appearances for club and country.

The 27-year-old has played at least 60 matches in each of the past four campaigns, prompting concerns among Arsenal supporters that he is at risk of burnout or injury.

Arteta kept Rice on the field for the full 90 minutes of Arsenal’s midweek victory over Slavia Prague but insisted the club is working harder than ever to manage the midfielder’s workload.

So far this season, Rice has been left out of Arsenal’s two Carabao Cup matches and also withdrew from the previous international break in September.

Asked if he was concerned about Rice’s fitness, Arteta said: “Concerns? Which is the only player, the only player in this squad, that for two games in the Carabao Cup has been left out of the squad? At home with two days off? It’s not true [that Rice is being overplayed].

“We are really looking after him more than any other season. The way he is training and all the love [he is being shown]. That’s it.

“Here are the demands of this football club and a player like him. Not only him, because there are many others that have even less time. That’s it. That has to be the mindset. If you start to put other things in your brain, [it will create] damage. Erase them, get them in the bin and just focus on what you have to do.”.

Newly-promoted Hull City stunned Arsenal at the Emirates thanks to goals from Geovanni and Daniel Cousin in September 2008, but you will find long odds on them repeating the feat this afternoon.

With Manchester City playing at Nottingham Forest in the later kick-off, Mikel Arteta’s team have the chance to extend their lead at the top of the Premier League and make it 27 points from a possible 30 going into the international break.

Victory at Anfield last weekend was achieved with steel and resolve, but the more intricate side of Arsenal’s attacking play will be under the microscope against opponents likely to defend deep and in numbers.

With that in mind, it was noteworthy that Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard, Bruno Guimaraes and Myles Lewis-Skelly started the Champions League win at Slavia Prague on the bench, with only Odegaard coming on.

Declan Rice played the full 90 minutes, and one wonders if this is a rare chance for Arteta to leave him out of a Premier League starting XI.

Hull are 12th and have lost only two league games, a performance which far exceeds the gloomy pre-season forecasts for their chances. However, they are winless since the end of August and have not kept a clean sheet since a goalless draw with Aston Villa on Sept 4.

There is one other three o’clock kick-off: Fulham host Newcastle United at Craven Cottage, with Matthias Jaissle under increasing pressure.

Newcastle were booed off at St James’ Park on Monday after their limp defeat by Everton, and have looked far too easy to play through all season, with their defensive statistics making for grim reading.

Industry observers note that alvaro Arbeloa was in Jaissle’s position a few weeks ago, but Fulham appear to have turned a corner and were impressive in a 1-1 at Villa Park last time out. There were reports of dressing room unrest, but Fulham rank highly for possession and chance creation so it appears the Spaniard is putting his stamp on things.

'I persuaded my club to give me a job as a content creator'

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If someone would've said to me I'd be doing this as a job when I was 12, I wouldn't have believed them.

My name's Jacob. I'm a content creator, and I work with Bolton Wanderers.

In a recent development, my role here at Bolton is coming up with fresh ideas for social media, to try new concepts, filming stuff, and then posting them onto Bolton's pages and trying to help people follow the club. In my opinion, I think it's one of the funnest jobs in football, and it's brilliant.

Right. Welcome to Bolton, Larra. I hope I remarked that right. I'm going to teach you some Bolton twang to help you settle in.

Sources indicate that my passion for football when I was growing up started at a very young age. My dad used to take me to the football matches, and I got my very first season ticket when I was five years old in the 2010/11 season, when Bolton was in the Premiership. Being something I loved as a kid, to turn it into my job is amazing.

I work here at least two days a week, obviously filming content, producing content,and then on match day, I'll be filming mostly with fans, and I love it.

Industry observers note that as a town? Well, for us, it's lovely. Yeah.

Mondays, meetings. We have the marketing meeting, so that gives you an idea of what the week holds, what I'm going to do on a match day with the fans. And then in the week, I either film in with players, retail, commercial,whatever department needs help producing videos.

Some of the skills I use, I think one of them's got to be communication. You've got to be able to talk to people, talk to fans, and if you're watching this and you're a bit shy, or you think you can't communicate with people as well, I was like that inhigh school, so you learn it as you get older. But working in football, you've got to be adaptable because one minute you're doing a new signing, next minute you're working with the players, next minute it's a match day, next minute the season's over.

It has been revealed that I'd say another one is being creative. That's probably the most crucial one because without being creative, you won't be able to put a video together.

So when I was 16 in high school, that's where my journey started. I did videos, which got me a number of followers. I always struggled in the classroom side in high school, but creating content and creating ideas and being creative, I was always really, really good at in high school, whether that would be doing something drama-related or English, writing, creating stories. I always knew I had a passion for creative pieces of work and being able to now do it as a job, it suits me down to the ground.

In a recent development, I didn't go to college. I didn't go to uni. I left high school with no GCSEs, but I've always had a real passion for football, so that's how I got in contact with Bolton Wanderers. I started doing some videos here at Bolton with the fans and that, and then it turned into going to the training ground and filming with the players, working with the commercial team, retail team, all the different departmentsaround the football club to eventually getting a paid role in football.

I think don't wait for an opportunity to come to you. Get out there and try. If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role there. But if it doesn't, then you've also created a portfolio working with different people, different businesses, different companies, and it's really good for your CV and for future opportunities with different companies.

The highlight of my career so far, probably looking back, being resilient enough to create my own career path in doing something I love.

When you score this season, you might be chuffed.

If you're passionate about football, you're a bit creative, and you're good in front of the camera, content creation infootball might be a job for you.

To find out what other careers you can have in football, explore the BBC Bitesize Follow Your Passion collection.

Making videos with fans and players at his local football club is all in a day's work for Jacob.

He's a content creator for Bolton Wanderers FC, coming up with newly introduced ideas for social media, filming videos and posting them onto official pages. The aim is to encourage people to follow the club.

According to recent reports, there are many different ways to develop a career in football content creation, from apprenticeships to freelance work and full-time employment. It isn't just about making videos - content creators need to understanding their audience, respond to analytics and adapt material for different platforms.

Jacob works as a content creator for Bolton Wanderers and his career progression has followed this path:.

Voluntary work at Bolton --> Professional content creator.

While it might look simple, he's had to be resilient - and one of the biggest obstacles he faced was convincing Bolton to create his role. "Don't wait for an opportunity to come to you," he states. "If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role. If it doesn't, you've created a portfolio and it's really good for your CV and future opportunities.".

It has been revealed that jacob says salaries can range from Â£26,000 to around Â£40,000 for roles like his. Like him, some content creators start by doing it as a hobby while they improve their skills. While some content creators are full-time employees, many are freelancers so their average salaries can be variable.

Find out more about the role of a content creator below. Content creation roles can come under a range of titles including social media manager or content manager.

You could get into this role via a college course (to get practical skills in video editing and production, or a T Level in Marketing), an apprenticeship, volunteering, short private training courses and also teaching yourself.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andoni Iraola's high press is yet to take its toll on the Liverpool squad after only 10 Premier League games, but there is every chance it will as the season wears on.

While the likes of Dominik Szoboszlai, Ryan Gravenberch and Alexis Mac Allister provide excellent press resistance and ball progression, for each of them to play 50-or-more games across all competitions in such a demanding system could prove untenable.

More urgent is that when the first wave of Liverpool's press is bypassed, the lack of a defensive shield leaves the backline exposed to central counter-attacks, which most notably occurred on the opening day of the upcoming season against Newcastle.

Sources indicate that if Liverpool are to maintain their competitive edge in the second half of the season, identifying a specialist No. 6 in the January transfer window is advisable.

In a recent development, according to a new data visualisation from Ballity Insight Lab analysing 68 LaLiga midfielders across the 2026/27 season, the profile Liverpool require is currently thriving in Spain. The below model plots 'duel destroyers' against 'ball-winners' seeking to find out which midfielders are good at both functions.

La Liga’s toughest midfielders? Duel Destroyer vs Ball Winner 📊 Wins it and wins duels: 🇦🇷 Guido Rodríguez, 🇪🇸 Rodri, 🇨🇴 Deossa, 🇫🇷 Camavinga, 🇪🇸 Gorrotxategi, 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Bellingham, 🇩🇰 Hjulmand, 🇪🇸 Bernal, 🇫🇷 Lemar, 🇪🇸 Barrios Formula in the comments 👇 https://t.co/6rcVRo63vUNovember 16, 2026.

The top-right quadrant of this scatter plot is categorised as the 'wins it and wins duels' bracket.

This zone is reserved for midfielders who consistently break up opposition play with lots of tackling and interceptions, whilst also dominating individual physical battles.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Unsurprisingly, the quadrant is populated by unattainable global stars such as Real Madrid duo Eduardo Camavinga and Jude Bellingham, alongside more established anchors like Guido Rodriguez and Morten Hjulmand.

However, just beneath those household names are two statistical outliers who could be January targets for the Anfield recruitment team: Jon Gorrotxategi and Nelson Deossa.

Gorrotxategi, who like Iraola is of Basque descent and presently represents Real Sociedad, stands out as the most compelling statistical fit for Liverpool’s needs.

The Spanish midfielder is positioned near the 95th percentile in the 'duel destroyer' category while simultaneously sitting around the 88th percentile as a ball-winner.

He boasts an aggressive, front-foot defensive style that would suit the demands of Premier League football.

The data suggests Gorrotxategi could function as Liverpool's midfield backstop, sweeping up loose balls and engaging opposition ball-carriers before they can reach the Reds' defensive third.

Deossa, meanwhile, presents an intriguing, slightly more balanced alternative, which perhaps Liverpool already have covered in their midfield stable.

The Colombian midfielder ranks just below the 90th percentile for ball-winning and hovers around the 85th percentile for duels. His profile suggests he is a player who reads the game well to block passing lanes, while retaining the physical bite required to win ground duels in the middle third.

Relying on converted No. 8s, or an up-and-coming 19-year-old, to anchor a title-challenging midfield is a compromise that opponents will punish as the season deepens. Liverpool need a player capable of holding central spaces when the full-backs push high and to win second balls from clearances.

The likes of Camavinga or Hjulmand may dominate mainstream transfer gossip columns this winter, but the smart money lies in targeting the anomalies.

In going for either Gorrotxategi or Real Betis man Deossa in January, Liverpool would acquire a midfield destroyer capable of plugging the gaps and protecting the defence, ultimately freeing their more technical midfielders to focus on unlocking opposition low blocks. Neither will come cheap, though, as both players are contracted to their respective clubs until June 2030.

Republic of Ireland have plenty of promise, but are unable to shake self-sabotage

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hopes of promotion remain alive, but another costly collapse has raised familiar questions before the decisive Nations League game with Kosovo.
  • The Republic of Ireland stand on the verge, although of what, nobody seems quite sure.
  • For 78 minutes in Linz on Saturday, Heimir Hallgrímsson’s side gave as good as they got against an Austria side who had not lost at home for a little more than three years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hopes of promotion remain alive, but another costly collapse has raised familiar questions before the decisive Nations League game with Kosovo.

The Republic of Ireland stand on the verge, although of what, nobody seems quite sure. Tuesday’s final Nations League group match, at home to Kosovo, presents a chance for progress or yet another opportunity to showcase a frustrating habit of messing things up.

For 78 minutes in Linz on Saturday, Heimir Hallgrímsson’s side gave as good as they got against an Austria side who had not lost at home for a little more than three years. Set up in a compact, attack-minded formation they carried credible threat against hosts managed by Ralf Rangnick, but to nobody’s great surprise Sasa Kalajdzic broke the deadlock, scrambling home the winner from a needlessly conceded and poorly defended corner.

This late lapse neatly captures the contradiction bedevilling this Ireland team under Hallgrímsson. Over the past 12 months, Ireland have been unmistakably better than they were during the dark days of the post-pandemic slump under Stephen Kenny. They have established a clear identity and pulled off a couple of phenomenal wins with a spine of players performing at an elite level, supplemented by emerging talent from the leagues below and beyond. Yet for all that, an acceptable level of success remains elusive for a team who have not managed to shake a maddening habit of self-sabotage.

It has been revealed that they have a high ceiling, as they demonstrated a year ago. Last November they dismantled Portugal at the Aviva Stadium in a World Cup qualifier before booking their place in the playoffs with an unforgettable come-from-behind win against Hungary at the Puskas Arena.

According to recent reports, in Budapest, the celebrations of a dramatic Troy Parrott hat-trick completed in the sixth minute of added time went viral and elevated the then AZ striker from being surplus to the requirements of a dreadful Tottenham to sought-after European household name. For the first time in almost a decade, Ireland were playing with something resembling swagger, spearheaded by a poster-boy striker apparently entering his prime.

Riding that wave, Ireland travelled to Prague last March for the playoff semi-final against Czechia, with Parrott striking again, from the penalty spot, as they set about taking an early 2-0 lead. What followed would become the lowest point of Hallgrímsson’s reign as Ireland sat back and invited pressure before conceding a needless penalty and subsequent late equaliser that preceded a crushing shootout defeat. Despite last summer’s expanded 48-team format in North America, poor game management had stymied Ireland’s chances of making the cut.

An uninspiring, but unbeaten, summer friendly window featured fairly routine low-profile wins over Grenada and Qatar and a 1-1 draw against the World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal. Having steadied the ship before this Nations League campaign, Ireland produced a performance in their opener against Kosovo little short of diabolical and went down to another late goal.

In the subsequent four fixtures, two overshadowed by loud protests over Ireland’s decision to honour matches against Israel, that same cycle of promise and frustration has played out on a loop.

The disappointment of defeat in Pristina was immediately cancelled out by a clinical dispatch of Israel in Debrecen. In Dublin, against Austria, Parrott struck twice to give Ireland a commanding first-half lead, but in a collapse that rather mirrored their nightmarish Prague experience, Ireland went on to relinquish control and were forced to settle for a disappointing draw.

Three days later they coughed up another lead in a bad-tempered 1-1 draw with Israel, their compulsion for throwing away cheap points from winning positions coming back to bite them. Although they never led against Austria on Saturday, when Caoimhín Kelleher made a series of excellent saves, the winner they conceded was ridiculously soft.

Hallgrímsson’s appointment in July 2024 after a drawn-out process lasting eight months came as a surprise. He has built a side with a strong, if occasionally gaffe-prone, backbone including Kelleher, the goalkeeper’s Brentford teammate Nathan Collins and the Ipswich defender Dara O’Shea. Jack Moylan, having the season of his life at Cardiff, has impressed in midfield, and Southampton’s Finn Azaz is an occasional, but unreliable, source of creative guile. Parrott, enjoying life in La Liga with Real Betis, has evolved from promising talent to undisputed focal point of the attack.

Sources indicate that to his credit, Hallgrímsson has forged a clear, pragmatic identity that maximises his team’s strengths without any delusions of fancy-dan footballing grandeur against elite opposition. Under his watch, Ireland are rarely outclassed and carry a cutting edge sorely absent in the dying days of his predecessor’s tenure.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, an inability to concentrate for 90 minutes continues to be their undoing and the must-win Nations League group finale at the Aviva Stadium will provide the ultimate judgment on the past 12 months. With Austria guaranteed promotion to League A, Ireland still have second place and its promotion playoff spot within reach.

According to recent reports, victory over Kosovo would also secure a place in pot two for next month’s Euro qualifying draw in Belfast, whereas defeat could leave them flirting with a relegation playoff to the tournament’s third tier. As the only ever-present residents of the Nations League’s second tier, now may be the time for something finally to give.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.
  • Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done. You find so much more out about yourself that you probably never knew.

Who are you and what is your job role?

Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.

What does a women's referee pathway officer do?

Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.

What kind of training do you give to aspiring referees?

So from going through recruitment courses first of all, and then we do the beginners course with referees, just giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge, then we will also do a practical part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we'll go through scenarios, positioning, things around free kick management for example, other set pieces likecorners, penalty setup, what you do as a referee day to day, even pre match stuff as well, so when you arrive at the grounds, how you check the pitch, check all the equipment is there, how you would interact with players, coaches and then just again, maybe createlike a role play sort of environment so that they know that they're not going totally blind into that sort of situation.

Have you always been passionate about football?

Football was a passion of mine, even when I was younger, primary school age, we just didn't have very many female teams, so it normally meant playing with the boys and the boys teams and stuff up until I was about 14, which was the minimum age here you can join senior ladies football team, which is what I did, and played there for 14 years at a club here locally, including up until the Women's Premiership, so it was great to be involved in football, but I always loved watching football, playing football, anything to do with football, I was always there and interested.

How did you go from playing football to being a referee?

Becoming a referee for me sort of happened by chance to be honest. It was during a game, one time I got an injury, quite a bad injury to my knee and then I had seen luckily that the referee course was being advertised. So I signed up for it, but I also signed up for a coaching course pretty much at the same time, maybe about six weeks apart. I wasnât really sure which role I wanted to follow, but over that winter I had been pushed into refereeing a wee bit and noted sure, why not, Iâll give it a go, it'd be a bit of extra fitness before my season restarts, and then just fell in love with it from there and never looked back.

What subjects did you study at school and university?

Coming through school I always picked PE, so I did my GCSE PE and then I also did A-level PE and then when I went onto university,I had the sport and exercise science as well within that, so I think it gives you a good understanding of obviously how your body works, and your proposal and training, stuff like that as well so you know when you're working nutrition wise, things that you need to know,especially as you reach the top level, just to make sure that you're getting the most out of your body.

What are your top tips for becoming a referee?

I would say definitely give it a try for sure. You never know until you do it. I think even when I was a player, I probably never imaginedthat I would be a referee and that I would even achieve and have experienced what Iâve been able to experience. So you never knowuntil you give it a go, but it's also about probably pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, being comfortable with being uncomfortable in situations like that. It's maybe not always as bad as it probably seems it's going to be. There's probably a lot more stigma around being a referee - who wants to be a referee? - but honestly for me, it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.

With a lifelong love of football, Louise Thompson followed her passion for the game, first as a player and now as a referee. As well as refereeing Fifa and NIFL Premiership matches, she also works for the Irish Football Association as the women's referee pathway officer, recruiting and developing up-and-coming female refs.

Louise Thompson on refereeing the Women's Irish Cup final.

Industry observers note that if you're interested in becoming a referee, it's something you can get involved with from a young age through local referee courses. The minimum age to become a qualified referee varies depending on where in the UK you live:.

In her role as a women's referee pathway officer, Louise oversees upcoming referees right from the initial recruitment courses stage: "We then do the beginners' course with referees, giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge," she notes. "We also do a hands-on part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we go through different scenariosâ¦ exactly what you do as a referee, and day-to-day practical stuff as wellâ¦ The idea is to give them all the basics and fundamentals before they go into a game so that they're prepared.".

All four UK nations have established pathways for referee development and progression. Starting out at grassroots level, it's possible to progress all the way to Fifa!

Sources indicate that louise's first games were youth games: "I still remember my first game to this day," she notes. "It was an under-13 game, and I was definitely the most nervous person on the pitch." She explains: "Over time, you'll get mentors who will come and watch you, give you advice, give you feedback" which will help you to progress to higher levels of the game.

As well as PE, Louise has found that languages are really helpful in this line of work, "especially when you're dealing with a lot of international games and people coming along," she says. "If you can learn some languages, it's very, very useful.".

You could get into this role by training with a professional body.

Sources: National Careers Service, GOV.UK, FA, IFA, SFA, and FAW.

Recent findings suggest that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Thomas Frank has teased that there is more to the story of his torrid time at Tottenham he will be willing to tell once he has steered Crystal Palace back on course.

The 53-year-old was prepared for plenty of questions about his past employers when he was unveiled to the media on Thursday afternoon ahead of Saturday’s trip to Coventry, acknowledging “I know today is a lot about me”.

The Danish boss helped stabilise Brentford in the Premier League, and was nominated for the league’s Manager of the Year award while with the Bees, but could not replicate the same success at Spurs and was sacked after just under eight months in charge.

“It’s something I’ve… maybe one day I’ll tell a little bit more about it,” said Frank, whose deal through June 2029 was declared on Monday.

“I understand why it’s also interesting. I think it’s more about Palace in general today. What can I say? I always said the day I got sacked, I’ll have time to travel, so I think I was relatively quick over it.

“But of course you want success, and I’m competitive, so I think that answer probably demands a little bit more time, which I am happy to do one day.”.

For now, Frank – who spent his time off in Japan, Australia and Denmark – has to figure out what to do with a side resuming their Premier League season in last place, while also balancing a Europa League campaign that continues next Thursday at home against Real Sociedad.

On Thursday, Palace confirmed two additions to the fresh boss’ backroom staff, with Justin Cochrane joining as first-team coach and Chris Haslam as fitness and athletic performance coach.

Cochrane worked with Frank at both Brentford and Tottenham, and is right now part of Thomas Tuchel’s England set-up, while Haslam was previously the head of athletic performance at Frank’s former employers Brentford, and also works as a fitness coach with the Danish FA.

Chelsea set-piece coach Bernardo Cueva was also confirmed as part of Frank’s team on Friday morning, with existing staff Paddy McCarthy, the assistant manager, and goalkeeping coach Andy Quy retained.

Frank is a firm believer that “culture is everything”, and boils down his philosophy to a “no dickheads” approach to crafting a cohesive, successful environment.

Asked about claims that his success at Brentford had more to do with the model, he replied: “Let’s put it this way: I think I was pretty important in terms of building that model.”.

He has no qualms about what he has witnessed so far from a squad he is still getting to know as many have recently returned from international duty.

Frank added: “The players were buzzing. That told me, ‘Oh, that’s good. They like to be together’. That’s very important, because it’s been tough times until now.

“Hopefully we can just continue, but there will also be ups and downs in games and whatever, and that’s why we need each other.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In 1967, Major Roy Bates, the owner of a pirate radio station, occupied HM Fort Roughs – a fortress in the North Sea, seven miles off the Suffolk coast – and declared it a nation.
  • Recent findings suggest that by 1975, Sealand had a flag, a constitution, an anthem and passports.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Principality of Sealand is only half the length of a football pitch, but that hasn't stopped the tiny micronation from trying to make its grand return to international football.

In 1967, Major Roy Bates, the owner of a pirate radio station, occupied HM Fort Roughs – a fortress in the North Sea, seven miles off the Suffolk coast – and declared it a nation.

Recent findings suggest that by 1975, Sealand had a flag, a constitution, an anthem and passports. Like any self-respecting country, it also needed a football team. The Sealand National Football.

In a recent development, association was first founded in 2003 – the entire national team was initially from Denmark, bizarrely – then revived by a Scot six years later, competing in non-FIFA matches against the likes of the Chagos Islands and Alderney. Fixtures weren't played on the offshore platform, but rather in Godalming, in Surrey. Royle Family actor Ralf Little was among those who played for the team, with former West Ham hard man Julian Dicks taking the coaching reins for a spell, before activities came to an end once more in the mid-2010s.

After a 12-year hiatus, Sealand is set to return in 2027 with both men's and women's ‘national sides', as well as a different approach.

“This team is all about spreading the message of Sealand, but we will be a proper international team ready to play other nations, both recognised and unrecognised,” director of football Ross Galbally tells FFT.

While it may appear that Sealand could struggle for a player pool (even Michael Bates, who inherited the platform from his dad, doesn't actually live there), anyone who takes up an e-citizenship of the Principality will be eligible for selection – that can be bought online for £7.99 a month, while noble titles are also available.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

It costs £499.99 to become a Duke or Duchess, but just £39.99 to become a Baron or Baroness – in 2012, Ed Sheeran became Baron von Edward Sheeran of Sealand.

“Sealand's motto is ‘From the sea, freedom,'” Galbally explains. “Our team is open to anyone sharing our values. Every other country picks on citizenship and birthright, so why can't we select our team based on values?”.

“THE WHOLE ADVENTURE IS ABOUT SEALAND AND ITS ETHOS, BUT ALSO THE PLAYERS' JOURNEYS”.

Sources indicate that the team's first trials will be held in early 2027, and people can apply from anywhere. There has already been interest from Argentina, the USA and Scandinavia.

In a recent development, “We hope Sealand will offer a second chance for players who missed out on showing their talent on the international stage,” Galbally notes. “This whole adventure is about Sealand and its ethos, but also the players, their stories and their journeys.”.

Sealand's managerial team is set to include coaches with experience in the EFL, as well as non-league. The executive board is a mixture of those with football backgrounds and people involved with music – a link to Sealand's pirate radio past.

The new team's inaugural game is likely to be in the UK, but matches could also take place in mainland Europe and the USA.

There are no plans to knock on FIFA or UEFA's door any time soon, and it also seems unlikely they'd meet the criteria to join CONIFA, the alternative organisation for nations, states and peoples not recognised by FIFA – current members of that organisation include Tibet, Greenland and Cornwall.

But Sealand has never been overly concerned about following the rules – from 2027, football's latest national side could be coming to a city near you.

Echoes of Azteca but not like Argentina: fearless England start afresh in Madrid
